per-croesus: King of Lydia, son of Alyattes, who subjugated the Greek cities of Asia Minor and the nations west of the Halys River, becoming the first foreigner to exact tribute from Greeks, until his conflict with Persia.
per-cambyses: Son of Cyaxares and father of Cyrus; a Persian of noble birth whom Astyages married to his daughter Mandane, believing him beneath Median rank.
per-astyages: King of Media, son of Cyaxares, deposed by Cyrus of Persia and brother-in-law to Croesus of Lydia through marriage arranged as part of a peace treaty between Lydia and Media.
per-heracles: A legendary Greek hero whose descendants, the Heraclidae, ruled Sardis according to Herodotus' genealogy; also a geographical marker (Pillars of Heracles) marking the boundary of the known world.
per-cyrus: Founder of the Persian empire, son of Cambyses, who destroyed the Median kingdom of Astyages and whose growing power prompted Croesus to consult the oracles and later invade Cappadocia.
per-darius: King of Persia (r. 522–486 BC), son of Hystaspes, who conquered Babylon and was known for his administrative reforms and building projects.
per-amasis: King of Egypt who made an alliance with Croesus against Persia and reigned when the Egyptians marked a transition in their pantheon.
per-mardonius: A Persian nobleman, son of Gobryas and cousin of Xerxes, who commanded an expedition to Greece in 492 BC that ended unsuccessfully when his army was wounded by the Brygi and his fleet damaged at Athos, and who later persuaded Xerxes to invade Greece as revenge for Persian defeats.
per-xerxes: King of the Persian Empire, son of Darius I, who took a golden statue from the Babylonian temple, killed its priest, and executed Sataspes for failing to complete a voyage around Libya.
per-cleomenes: Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides held the kingship of Sparta by right of birth, showed integrity in refusing bribes from Maeandrius, and reigned for a relatively short time before dying without a male heir.
per-harpagus: A Mede and trusted administrator in Astyages' household who, ordered to kill the infant Cyrus, instead arranged for the child's safety, and later advised Cyrus on military tactics against Croesus at Sardis.
per-histiaeus: Tyrant of Miletus who, at a council of Ionian rulers, advised against revolt from Darius and in favor of breaking the bridge over the Ister to prevent Scythian crossing, thereby earning Darius' favor and a grant of Myrcinus in Thrace, which he subsequently began to fortify.
per-polycrates: Tyrant of Samos, son of Aeaces, who seized power by deposing his brothers, amassed great wealth and military strength (150 triremes and 1000 archers), conquered islands and mainland cities including Lesbios, and maintained a diplomatic alliance with Amasis of Egypt.
per-zeus: Chief deity of the Greek pantheon, invoked by Croesus in his grief, recognized by the Persians as the sky itself and worshipped on mountaintops, and honored by both Greeks and Persians as a recipient of sacred offerings and oaths.
per-themistocles: Athenian general and political leader who persuaded Athens to build a fleet by interpreting the Delphic Oracle favorably for naval warfare and served as commander of Athenian forces at Tempe during Xerxes' invasion.
per-aristagoras: A deputy ruler of Miletus, son of Molpagoras and son-in-law of Histiaeus, who proposed to the Persian satrap Artaphrenes an expedition to conquer Naxos and the Cycladic islands.
per-pausanias: Spartan general and guardian of King Pleistarchus, who commanded the Greek forces at Plataea and later became controversial for his autocratic behavior; son of Cleombrotus.
per-pisistratus: Tyrant of Athens, son of Hippocrates; he seized power by raising a third faction during internal Athenian strife, was initially expelled, and was restored to rule through the support of Megacles, governing the city according to its established laws and constitution.
per-smerdis: Son of Cyrus and brother of Cambyses, whom Cambyses sent to Persia and had killed by Prexaspes out of fear that Smerdis would seize the throne after a prophetic dream.
per-herodotus: Author of the Histories, an Ionian Greek from Halicarnassus who traveled widely and inquired into the origins of the Greco-Persian Wars.
per-demaratus: Son of Ariston and co-king of Sparta with Cleomenes, of the junior royal house (Agiad line); he opposed Cleomenes' arrest of Aeginetans by letter to Crius and later suffered deposition engineered by Cleomenes through charges relating to his father Ariston's third marriage.
per-miltiades: Athenian general and tyrant of the Chersonese at the Hellespont, son of Cimon; he advised the Ionians to revolt against Darius but was overruled, and his family had earlier established rule there through the Dolonci when his father Cypselus accepted their invitation.
per-apollo: Greek god of music, prophecy, and healing, through whose oracle Croesus learned he should make Greeks his friends, and for whose statue at Thornax in Laconia the Lacedaemonians received gold from Croesus.
per-leonidas: King of Sparta and commander of the Greek forces at Thermopylae, who died defending the pass against Xerxes' invading Persian army.
per-dionysus: A god worshipped by the Ethiopians alongside Zeus, to whom the people of Meroe attribute their military decisions through divine oracle.
per-athena: Greek goddess of wisdom, warfare, and crafts; invoked in oracles and religious contexts throughout the narrative, including the temple at Assesos in Milesian territory and the Athenian acropolis.
per-otanes: A Persian nobleman and courtier, son of Pharnaspes, who discovered that the supposed Smerdis ruling Persia was actually a Magus impostor by learning the usurper lacked ears, and initiated the conspiracy with other Persian nobles to expose and overthrow him.
per-alexander: Son of Amyntas, king of Macedonia, who in his youth nearly provoked a conflict with Persian envoys at his father's court.
per-ariston: One of two Spartan kings during the reign of Croesus, serving jointly with Anaxandrides; father of Demaratus.
per-cleisthenes: An Alcmaeonid of Athens who, after losing a power struggle with Isagoras, reorganized the Athenian tribes from four to ten and took the commons into his party to strengthen his position, thereby laying groundwork for democratic reform.
per-helen: The Spartan wife of Menelaus, daughter of Tyndarus, whose abduction by Paris (Alexandrus) precipitated the Trojan War, though according to Egyptian priests she was detained in Egypt by King Proteus while Paris sailed on.
per-periander: Tyrant of Corinth, son of Cypselus; a close friend of Thrasybulus of Miletus, to whom he disclosed an oracle's response about Alyattes, and who later tested the truth of Arion the lyre-player's miraculous rescue by a dolphin and took revenge on Samos for their refusal to allow him to send Corcyraean boys
per-psammetichus: King of Egypt who halted Scythian invasion through diplomatic gifts and prayers, and conducted an early linguistic experiment attempting to discover which people were oldest.
per-gelon: Tyrant of Gela and later Syracuse in Sicily, whose power exceeded all other Greek states; Greeks sent envoys to solicit his aid against Xerxes' invasion.
per-gyges: A Lydian bodyguard and favorite of King Candaules, forced by the king's wife to murder his master and seize the throne of Lydia after being made to witness her naked.
per-artaphrenes: Governor of Sardis and overseer of Persian coastal territories in Asia, appointed by King Darius to exercise authority over the peoples of the coast; he agrees to support Aristagoras' plan to attack Naxos with a large naval force.
per-prexaspes: A trusted Persian courtier of Cambyses who secretly killed the king's brother Smerdis on his orders and later saw his own son shot through the heart when Cambyses sought to prove his sanity.
per-oroetes: Persian governor of Sardis appointed by Cyrus, who plotted to destroy Polycrates of Samos out of wounded pride and successfully lured him to his death by false promises of shared treasure.
per-apries: Pharaoh of Egypt, son of Psammis, who reigned for twenty-five years and was eventually overthrown by the rebel Amasis after a disastrous military expedition against Cyrene provoked Egyptian mutiny.
per-artabanus: Uncle of Darius and Xerxes, son of Hystaspes; a Persian counselor who advised against Darius' Scythian campaign and later opposed Xerxes' invasion of Greece, only to be rebuked and excluded from the expedition.
per-hephaestus: A god venerated at Memphis, whose temple served as a source of information for Herodotus' Egyptian accounts.
per-alyattes: King of Lydia (r. 619–560 BC), son of Sadyattes, who waged war against the Medes and Cimmerians, conquered Smyrna and attacked Miletus for eleven years before making peace after consulting the Delphic oracle about a temple he had burned.
per-megabazus: A Persian commander whom Darius greatly honored and left in charge of eighty thousand troops in Europe after his Balkan campaign, tasked with subduing all peoples of the Hellespont and Thrace who would not submit to Persian rule.
per-battus: Founder and king of Cyrene; son of Polymnestus (or according to Cyrenaean tradition, son of Phronime), a Theraean descendant of Euphemus whom the Delphic oracle commanded to establish a settlement in Libya, and whom Thera appointed as leader of its colonizing expedition.
per-artemis: Greek goddess of the hunt and wild animals, venerated throughout Egypt with major festivals at Bubastis (where she is identified with the Egyptian Bubastis) and elsewhere, and with an oracle at Buto.
per-adrastus: Son of Gordias (grandson of Midas) of Phrygia who, having accidentally killed his brother, sought purification and refuge with Croesus at Sardis, then fatally struck Croesus' son Atys with a misdirected spear while hunting the Mysian boar.
per-ethiopian: A type of stone used by Egyptian embalmers for cutting; also mentioned as a material characteristic of both Egyptian and Ethiopian equipment in representations of Sesostris.
per-leutychides: King of Sparta who succeeded Demaratus, led a military expedition to Thessaly where he accepted a bribe and was subsequently banished, and later accompanied Cleomenes in seizing Aeginetan hostages at Athens.
per-hippocrates: Father of Pisistratus the tyrant of Athens, himself an Athenian of distinguished lineage whose miraculous sacrifice at Olympia prompted the Lacedaemonian Chilon to prophesy that his son would become a tyrant.
per-artabazus: A Persian general, son of Pharnaces, who commanded the Parthians and Chorasmians in Xerxes' invasion army, escorted the king back to Asia after Salamis with sixty thousand men, and subsequently besieged and subdued revolted Greek cities in Pallene and Macedonia.
per-democedes: A physician from Croton, captured among the slaves of Oroetes after Polycrates' death, who healed Darius' injured foot and became famous throughout the Persian court.
per-perseus: A figure of Greek mythology (son of Danae), worshipped in the Egyptian city of Khemmis in the Theban district, where locals claim he appears and whose sandal, when found, brings prosperity to all Egypt.
per-arcesilaus: King of Cyrene, son of Battus the Founder; he ruled for sixteen years and was later strangled by his brother Learchus after a disastrous military campaign against Libyan forces.
per-masistes: Son of Darius and Atossa, Persian general commanding a division of Xerxes' army alongside the fleet, who after the Persian defeat at Mykale confronted the admiral Artayntes and nearly died in their dispute before being saved by Xenagoras of Halicarnassus.
per-demeter: Demeter is the Greek name Herodotus equates with the Egyptian goddess Isis, associated with grain.
per-hystaspes: An Achaemenid Persian of high standing, father of Darius, whom Cyrus suspected of plotting against him after a prophetic dream, though the vision in fact foreshadowed Darius's succession to the Persian throne.
per-hippias: Elder son of Pisistratus the Athenian tyrant, whose opinion prevailed in favor of recovering their family's sovereignty after exile, and who later ruled Athens as tyrant until driven out by the Alcmeonidae and Spartans.
per-gobryas: One of the seven Persian conspirators who overthrew the Magian usurper; he wrestled with the Magus in the dark chamber while Darius delivered the fatal blow, and later offered a dissenting interpretation of the Scythian gifts to Darius.
per-anaxandrides: King of Sparta (r. ca. 560–520 BC), father of Cleomenes; after initial failure against Tegea, the Spartans under his kingship defeated them and recovered the bones of Orestes; compelled by the ephors to take a second wife to produce an heir.
per-amyntas: King of Macedonia who submitted to Persian demands for earth and water from Megabazus' messengers, but whose son Alexander later killed them to prevent their assault on Macedonian women.
per-maeandrius: Scribe and administrator of Polycrates who later ruled Samos after his master's death; he initially promised to establish equality but instead seized power, imprisoned the citizens, and was eventually forced to evacuate the island when the Persians restored Syloson.
per-pactyes: A Lydian entrusted by Cyrus with the gold of Croesus and Sardis, who revolted against Persian rule, hired mercenaries, besieged the Persian governor Tabalus in the acropolis, and became the object of Cyrus' pursuit.
per-eurybiades: Spartan admiral commanding the Greek fleet at Artemisium and Salamis, persuaded by bribes from Themistocles to stand and fight rather than retreat.
per-poseidon: Greek god of the sea, worshipped by Ionians at the Panionion on Mykale, by Libyans from ancient times, and by Scythians as Thagimasadas, though unknown to the Egyptians.
per-dorieus: Son of Anaxandrides, king of Sparta; rejected as heir in favor of his younger half-brother Cleomenes, he led colonization expeditions first to Libya and then to Sicily, where he died fighting beyond the oracle's instructions.
per-syloson: Brother of Polycrates, tyrant of Samos; exiled by Polycrates, he gifted his cloak to Darius in Egypt and later petitioned the now-king Darius to restore him to Samos, which Darius granted through a military expedition.
per-solon: An Athenian lawgiver who, after establishing laws for Athens, traveled abroad for ten years including to Egypt and Sardis, where he famously told Croesus that no mortal can be called fortunate until death.
per-deioces: Founder of the Median monarchy who rose to power through practicing justice as a judge in his town, eventually becoming king of Media and uniting the previously divided Median towns under his rule.
per-aphrodite: A goddess worshipped at Ascalon in Syria (with temples in Cyprus and Cythera derived from it), identified by Persians with Mylitta of the Assyrians and Alilat of the Arabians, whose temple at Ascalon was plundered by Scythians who were thereafter afflicted with a "female" sickness, and to whom Babylonian women were required
per-ares: The Greek god of war, worshipped in Egypt at Papremis with an annual festival involving ritual combat, and venerated by the Scythians who uniquely made images, altars, and shrines in his honor.
per-aristeas: A poet of Proconnesus who claimed mystical possession by Apollo and composed the *Arimaspea*, describing northern lands beyond the Scythians; according to legend he died and disappeared mysteriously, reappearing years later.
per-sesostris: An Egyptian king who, according to priestly accounts, conquered territories from the Red Sea through Asia and into Europe, leaving commemorative pillars and rock carvings to mark his subjugations.
per-hera: A Greek goddess, wife of Zeus and protector of Argos; venerated in a festival where Cleobis and Biton honored her by drawing their mother's wagon to her temple, and whose shrine in Samos housed a bronze bowl intended as a gift to Croesus.
per-psammenitus: Last pharaoh of Egypt's 26th Dynasty, son of Amasis; defeated and captured by Cambyses II after reigning six months, then subjected to psychological torment by the Persian king who was impressed by his stoic response to his daughter's enslavement and son's threatened execution.
per-artemisia: Queen of Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyros, and Calydnos, who commanded five ships in Xerxes' invasion fleet of Greece, distinguished herself by advising against a naval battle at Salamis and by ramming an allied Calyndian vessel during the battle, gaining high favor with the Persian king.
per-cyaxares: King of the Medes, son of Phraortes and descendant of Deioces, who waged war against Alyattes of Lydia and was the father of Astyages (who was later conquered by Cyrus the Persian).
per-alexandrus: Son of Priam, who abducted Helen from Sparta and was blown by storm to Egypt, where King Proteus detained him and Helen until Menelaus could retrieve them.
per-aristodemus: Legendary founder-king of Sparta, son of Aristomachus; he led the Lacedaemonians to their historical land and fathered twin sons Eurysthenes and Procles through his wife Argeia, though he died before witnessing their succession dispute.
per-cadmus: Legendary founder of Thebes who brought Phoenician customs (particularly the worship of Dionysus) to Boeotia, father of Semele.
per-hydarnes: A Persian of high rank, one of the seven conspirators against the Magus, and later father of Sisamnes (commander of the Arians under Xerxes) and of Hydarnes the Immortals general.
per-thrasybulus: Tyrant of Miletus who, forewarned by Periander of Corinth that King Alyattes of Lydia would attack during a temple rebuilding, deceived Alyattes' herald by displaying abundance in the marketplace to make peace, and later counseled Periander through symbolic action (cutting wheat) on tyrannical rule.
per-megacles: An Athenian aristocrat, leader of the coastal faction, who allied with Pisistratus by offering his daughter in marriage to restore him to power.
per-glaucus: Glaucus of Chios, said to be the sole discoverer of iron-welding, who crafted the great silver bowl on an iron stand dedicated by Alyattes at Delphi.
per-candaules: Last Heraclid king of Sardis, who was overthrown and killed by his bodyguard Gyges after forcing Gyges to view his wife naked, an act that shamed her and led to her revenge.
per-isis: An Egyptian goddess worshipped throughout Egypt, identified by Herodotus with the Greek Demeter, honored with major festivals at Busiris and elsewhere, and depicted in female form with cow horns like Io.
per-amompharetus: Leader of the Pitanate battalion of Sparta, who initially refused to retreat from the barbarians at Plataea and cast a pebble-vote against withdrawal before eventually following Pausanias and the Lacedaemonian army.
per-cypselus: Tyrant of Corinth, son of Eetion; named after the chest in which his mother hid him at birth, he seized power at Corinth fulfilling an oracle from Delphi, ruled as a tyrant killing and exiling many Corinthians, and fathered Periander who succeeded him.
per-eetion: Father of Labda and husband of the Bacchiad woman; a Lapithian from Petra who received an oracle from Delphi predicting that his son would become a tyrant and bring justice to Corinth, though the Bacchiadae sent men to kill the child.
per-zopyrus: A Persian general, son of Megabyzus, who devised a stratagem to deliver Babylon to Darius by mutilating himself, feigning desertion, and coordinating a coordinated assault on the city's gates from within.
per-menelaus: Spartan king whose wife Helen was abducted by Alexandrus (Paris), and who according to Egyptian priests journeyed to Egypt to recover her from King Proteus after the Trojan War.
per-scyles: A Scythian king, son of Ariapithes by an Istrian mother, who adopted Greek customs while ruling and was eventually executed by his own people for abandoning Scythian ways.
per-apis: A sacred bull venerated by Egyptians as a manifestation of the god Epaphus, marked by specific physical signs and kept in a temple court at Memphis, whom Cambyses wounded and killed in a fit of rage.
per-atossa: Daughter of Cyrus, wife successively of her brother Cambyses, the Magus, and Darius; she consulted the physician Democedes about a breast ailment.
per-alcmeon: An Athenian aristocrat of the Alcmeonidae family, son of Megacles, who gained wealth and fame by assisting Croesus' envoys at Delphi and subsequently receiving a gift of gold from the Lydian king.
per-onesilus: King of Salamis in Cyprus who led a revolt against Persian rule, calling in Ionian support; he was killed in battle against the Persian general Artybius.
per-proteus: An Egyptian ruler of Memphis who detained Paris (Alexandrus) and Helen when they arrived in Egypt, safeguarding Helen and Paris's plundered wealth until the Greeks could recover them, and granting Paris safe passage to leave despite his violation of guest-friendship.
per-cimon: Father of Miltiades and Stesagoras; an Athenian who won Olympic victories with his chariot team but was exiled by Pisistratus, granted return after ceding a victory to Pisistratus, and was later murdered by Pisistratus' sons near the town-hall.
per-artayctes: Persian governor of Sestus on the Hellespont under Xerxes, who desecrated the temple of Protesilaus at Elaeus and was crucified by the Athenians under Xanthippus after the siege of Sestus.
per-pisistratidae: The family of Athenian tyrants who ruled Athens for thirty-six years until driven out by Spartan intervention and internal capture of their children, after which they withdrew to Sigeum on the Scamander.
per-heraclidae: Descendants of Heracles who held the kingship of Sardis for twenty-two generations until displaced by Gyges and the Mermnadae dynasty.
per-datis: A Mede and general appointed by Darius to lead the Persian invasion of Athens and Eretria, who showed unusual piety toward Delos and was credited with returning a stolen image of Apollo to its temple.
per-tomyris: Queen of the Massagetae whose husband was dead, she rejected Cyrus' marriage proposal and defeated his army at the Araxes River.
per-cleombrotus: Son of Anaxandrides, Spartan king; brother of Cleomenes, Dorieus, and Leonidas; passed over in succession to the kingship.
per-rhodopis: A Thracian courtesan, slave of Iadmon the Samian, freed in Egypt by Kharaxus of Mytilene (brother of Sappho), who became famous for dedicating iron spits at Delphi and whose name later Greeks wrongly associated with a pyramid built centuries before her time.
per-pheretime: Mother of Arcesilaus II of Cyrene; after her son's death at Barce, she fled to Egypt and secured Persian military aid from Aryandes to avenge him, personally overseeing brutal reprisals against the Barcaeans who had killed him.
per-hegesistratus: A diviner from Elis, hired by Mardonius to conduct sacrifices for the Persian army at Plataea; a former Spartan prisoner who had escaped by cutting off his own foot, and was later killed by the Lacedaemonians at Zacynthus.
per-evenius: Father of the prophet Deiphonus; a watchman of Apollonia's sacred solar flock who was blinded by his city for sleeping at his post, then compensated with estates and subsequently granted the gift of divination.
per-megabates: A Persian of the Achaemenid family and cousin to Artaphrenes and Darius, appointed general of the expedition against Naxios in 499 BC; his quarrel with Aristagoras over the flogging of Scylax led him to warn the Naxians of the coming attack, causing the campaign's failure.
per-arion: A lyric poet and citharode from Methymna who invented the dithyramb, and was saved by a dolphin after a Corinthian ship's crew tried to rob and kill him at sea.
per-anacharsis: A Scythian of royal descent who traveled widely, learned Greek customs, attempted to worship the Mother of the Gods in Scythia upon his return, and was killed by King Saulius for adopting foreign practices.
per-pythia: The priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracular responses to the Lacedaemonians regarding their conflicts with Tegea and to the Thracian Dolonci regarding their settlement in the Chersonese.
per-epialtes: A Malian who revealed to Xerxes the mountain path that allowed the Persians to outflank the Greek hoplites at Thermopylae, earning him a death sentence from Sparta and eventual assassination by an Trachinian named Athenades.
per-etearchus: King of the Ammonians who reported to visitors from Cyrene a story told him by Nasamonians about young men who crossed the Libyan desert and encountered a pygmy people and a river he identified as the Nile.
per-aeaces: Father of Polycrates; tyrant of Samos who was deposed, and grandfather of the later tyrant Aeaces.
per-achaemenes: Achaemenes was the brother of Xerxes and son of Darius; he was appointed governor of Egypt after its subjugation but was later killed by the Libyan Inaros.
per-tisamenus: Ancestor of Argeia (wife of Aristodemus) and thus great-grandfather of the Spartan twin kings Eurysthenes and Procles; son of Thersander and descendant of Polynices.
per-hipparchus: Son of Pisistratus and brother of the tyrant Hippias, he was slain by Aristogiton and Harmodius during the Panathenaea festival at Athens, an event that intensified rather than ended Athenian tyranny.
per-atys: Son of Croesus, king of Lydia, prophesied to die by an iron spear; killed by the guest Adrastus during a boar hunt on Mount Olympus.
per-leotychides: Spartan king who succeeded Demaratus after Cleomenes orchestrated his deposition by challenging his legitimacy, then insulted the deposed Demaratus at the Gymnopaidia, provoking him to exile among the Medes.
per-minos: A legendary Cretan king, son of Europa, who ruled the island in ancient times and subjected various peoples including the Carians to his authority, maintaining naval power.
per-aryandes: Persian viceroy of Egypt appointed by Cambyses, who at Pheretime's request sent forces that avenged Arcesilaus by besieging and enslaving Barce, but was later executed by Darius as a rebel after minting silver coinage of unprecedented purity in imitation of the king's gold coinage.
per-lycurgus: Athenian aristocrat, leader of the faction of the plain, whose feud with Megacles' coastal faction enabled Pisistratus' rise, and who later joined Megacles in driving him out after his first seizure of power.
per-melampus: A legendary Greek seer and healer from Pylos who introduced to the Greeks the worship of Dionysus and the phallic procession learned from Egypt, and who famously cured the madness of the women of Argos in exchange for a share of the kingdom.
per-megabyzus: A Persian of high rank, son of Otanes' trusted associate Gobryas; one of the seven conspirators against the Magus who debated forms of government and advocated for oligarchic rule, and father of Zopyrus.
per-mycerinus: King of Egypt, son of Kheops, renowned for his justice and clemency toward his people, who honored his deceased daughter with a gilded wooden cow shrine at Saïs.
per-callias: An Elean diviner of the Iamid clan who aided Croton against Sybaris, fleeing from the tyrant Telys because he could obtain no favorable omens while sacrificing for Sybaris' victory.
per-isagoras: An Athenian aristocrat of notable family who, after losing a power struggle with Cleisthenes, conspired with the Spartan king Cleomenes to seize control of Athens, but was repelled when the Athenians united against them on the acropolis.
per-theras: A Spartan regent descended from Polynices who, after ruling during his nephews' childhood, led colonists from Lacedaemon to the island of Calliste (later called Thera after him) to join Phoenician descendants already settled there.
per-priam: King of Troy whose son Alexander (Paris) abducted Helen, thereby causing the Trojan War; Herodotus cites Egyptian priests' claim that Helen never reached Troy, arguing that Priam would have returned her to avoid destruction of his city and loss of his sons.
per-artembares: A notable Mede whose son was whipped by the young Cyrus for disobedience during a children's game, and who complained to King Astyages about the outrage.
per-osiris: Egyptian god of the underworld and fertility, identified by Herodotus with the Greek Dionysus, worshipped throughout Egypt alongside Isis.
per-aeacus: A legendary hero, son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina, venerated by both Aeginetans and Athenians as a protector and ally in their conflicts with each other and against the Persians.
per-masistius: Commander of the Persian cavalry under Mardonius at Plataea, killed in battle when thrown from his horse and struck in the eye by the Greeks, mourned greatly by the Persian army as second only to Mardonius in esteem.
per-pythius: A wealthy Lydian of Atys who entertained Xerxes' army with lavish hospitality and offered financial support for the Persian invasion of Greece, but was brutally punished when he requested exemption for his eldest son from military service.
per-amestris: Wife of Xerxes, who wove a mantle for him, learned of his affair with Artaynte, and plotted to destroy Masistes' wife in revenge; in old age she buried fourteen notable Persian youths as an offering to the underworld god.
per-king-darius: King of Persia who rules over vast territories, punishes conspirators and disloyal governors including Intaphrenes and Oroetes, and whose authority is exercised through written orders and appointed officials throughout his empire.
per-hecataeus: Historian and adviser from Miletus who opposed the Ionian revolt against Persia, citing Darius's overwhelming power, but when overruled counseled seizing treasure from Branchidae to fund a naval campaign, and later advised Aristagoras to fortify Leros as a base of operations.
per-hyperboreans: A legendary people dwelling beyond Scythia at the world's edge, known to Greeks chiefly through Delian tradition of gift-offerings and sacred maidens sent to Delos.
per-intaphrenes: One of the seven Persian conspirators against the Magi who lost an eye fighting them but survived, later executed for mutilating palace gatekeepers when denied access to the king.
per-procles: Procles, sovereign of Epidaurus and maternal grandfather of Periander's sons, deliberately estranged the younger boy Lycophron from his father by revealing that Periander had killed their mother, prompting Periander to invade Epidaurus and imprison him.
per-artybius: A Persian general commanding forces against the Cypriot and Ionian rebels, killed in single combat by Onesilus at Salamis when the Carian attendant of Onesilus hamstrung his war-horse.
per-salmoxis: A Thracian (or Getae) deity worshipped for immortality, though Greeks claimed he was formerly a slave of Pythagoras who used deception and an underground chamber to convince his countrymen of eternal life.
per-thersander: Ancestor of the Spartan royal line, great-grandson of Polynices and father of Tisamenus, through whom descent from Cadmus passed to later Spartan kings.
per-hippocleides: An Athenian of great wealth and beauty, son of Tisandrus, leading suitor for the hand of Cleisthenes' daughter until he danced himself out of favor by performing indecorous dances at the marriage feast.
per-cimmerian: A nomadic people inhabiting the region north of the Black Sea and the Caucasus who, when driven westward by the Scythians, invaded Ionia and raided Greek cities before being displaced from their homeland.
per-stesagoras: Grandfather of Miltiades the Marathon general; father of Cimon; early ruler of the Chersonese whose line continued to govern the region.
per-aristodicus: A leading citizen of Cyme who twice questioned the oracle at Branchidae about whether to surrender the Lydian suppliant Pactyes to the Persians, and who symbolically challenged the god's consistency by removing birds from the temple.
per-triton: A sea-god of Libya who dwelt in the Tritonian lake and aided Jason's Argo by revealing the channel through the shallows in exchange for a bronze tripod.
per-leto: A goddess worshipped in Egypt at Buto, where she has an oracle and a great shrine of stone; in Egyptian theology she served as nurse to Apollo and Artemis.
per-hermes: Greek god of commerce, travel, and thieves, worshipped by various peoples including Egyptians (who had a city named after him) and certain Thracian peoples; venerated especially by Thracian nobility as their ancestor.
per-amphiaraus: A legendary Greek seer and hero whose oracle at an unnamed sanctuary received consultation from Croesus, who also dedicated a golden shield and spear to him at his shrine, where these offerings remained in the Theban temple of Ismenian Apollo until Herodotus' time.
per-danae: Mother of Perseus; in Greek mythology, she was imprisoned in a bronze tower and bore Perseus to Zeus, and the Egyptians of Khemmis claimed descent from her through Perseus and Danaus.
per-oebares: A Persian groom of Darius who used a trick involving a mare to ensure Darius' horse would neigh first at sunrise, thereby securing the kingship for Darius; later served as governor of Dascyleum under Xerxes' reign.
per-oeobazus: A Persian from Cardia who managed the bridge equipment at Sestus; killed by the Apsinthians while fleeing after the fortress fell to the Greeks, and father of Siromitres, a commander in Xerxes' army.
per-perdiccas: Founder of the Macedonian royal line who obtained tyranny there through a portent involving miraculous bread and sunlight, ancestor of Alexander I.
per-alcmeonidae: An aristocratic Athenian family, banished by the Pisistratidae, who attempted military return, financed the reconstruction of the Delphic temple, and ultimately secured Athens' liberation from tyranny through persuading the Lacedaemonian oracle.
per-hyllus: Ancestor of the Spartan royal houses, son of Heracles and founder of the line from which both Leonidas and Leutychides descended.
per-gorgus: King of Salamis in Cyprus, son of Chersis; he lost his throne to his younger brother Onesilus during the Ionian Revolt but was restored by the Salaminians and later served as a naval commander under Xerxes.
per-io: Daughter of Inachus, king of Argos, seized by Phoenician traders and carried to Egypt, whose abduction the Persians cited as the first wrong in the conflict between Greeks and barbarians.
per-artayntes: A Persian officer, son of Ithamitres, commander of the Pactyes contingent in Xerxes' invasion army, and later co-admiral of the Persian fleet at Samos who escaped after the battle of Plataea.
per-artachaees: A Persian of Achaemenid lineage, son of Artaeus, joint overseer with Bubares of the digging of the canal through Mount Athos during Xerxes' invasion of Greece, whom Xerxes honored greatly after his death and whose memory the Acanthians later revered as a hero.
per-polycritus: Son of Crius, an Aeginetan who initially resisted Spartan arrest on his island and later distinguished himself as one of the most courageous Greek naval fighters at Salamis, ramming enemy ships.
per-panionius: A Chian trader who castrated boys and sold them as eunuchs to Persian masters, including Hermotimus, whom he later encountered and was forced to castrate his own sons and be castrated by them in retribution.
per-xanthippus: Athenian statesman and general, son of Ariphron, father of Pericles, who prosecuted Miltiades, commanded Athenian forces at Salamis and the Hellespont, and captured Sestus from the Persians.
per-achaemenid: A Persian royal clan descended from Achaemenes; members held positions of power under Cyrus, Cambyses, and Xerxes.
per-thales: A Milesian mathematician and natural philosopher who predicted a solar eclipse to the Ionians and is credited by some with engineering the crossing of the river Halys for Croesus' army against the Persians.
per-necos: King of Egypt, son of Psammetichus, who began the canal project from the Nile to the Red Sea (later completed by Darius the Persian) before abandoning it upon a prophetic warning, and who defeated the Syrians at Magdolus and captured Cadytis.
per-amphitryon: Father of Heracles in Greek tradition, mentioned by Herodotus as evidence that the name Heracles came to Greece from Egypt rather than originating there, and as a dedicator of votive tripods at Thebes.
per-king-xerxes: Persian Great King who ruled the Achaemenid Empire and led the massive invasion of Greece in 480 BC, appearing throughout Herodotus' account as the supreme authority enforcing imperial justice and commanding military operations.
per-moeris: An ancient Egyptian king whose reign was approximately nine hundred years before Herodotus' visit, remembered for constructing a lake (subsequently called Lake Moeris), building pyramids, and erecting the northern forecourt of the temple of Hephaestus.
per-mitrobates: A Persian governor of Dascyleium who taunted Oroetes about his failure to conquer Samos, and was later killed by Oroetes during the reign of the Magi.
per-phanes: A Halicarnassian mercenary in Amasis' service who defected to Persia, advised Cambyses on the invasion route to Egypt, and was punished by the Egyptian mercenaries killing his sons before the final battle.
per-bagaeus: A Persian of royal blood, son of Artontes; selected by lot to carry forged letters from Darius to Sardis, where he used them to turn the spearmen against the satrap Oroetes, securing his execution and atonement for the death of Polycrates the Samian.
per-kheops: An Egyptian king who succeeded Rhampsinitus, compelled the entire population to labor for ten years building roads and underground chambers before constructing his great pyramid over twenty years, and was remembered as a tyrant who closed temples and enslaved the people.
per-sitalces: A Thracian king, son of Tereus, who negotiated the exchange of Scyles and Octamasades at the Ister and later betrayed Spartan ambassadors to the Athenians.
per-belus: Son of Ninus and ancestor of Alcaeus in the genealogy of early Lydian kings.
per-timoxenus: A general of the Scionaeans who conspired to betray Potidaea to the Persian Artabazus during his campaign, discovered when an arrow carrying their correspondence struck a Potidaean soldier instead of its intended recipient.
per-protesilaus: A Greek hero, son of Iphiclus, whose tomb and sacred precinct at Elaeus in the Chersonese contained treasure that the Persian Artayctes desecrated and plundered during Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
per-melanippus: A Theban hero, son of Astacus, brought to Sicyon by the tyrant Cleisthenes to supplant the worship of Adrastus, his mortal enemy whom he had slain in battle; also mentioned as a friend of the poet Alcaeus.
per-boreas: The north wind, husband of the Athenian princess Orithyia and considered son-in-law to Athens, whom the Athenians invoked for aid against the Persian fleet during the naval campaign.
per-hermotimus: A eunuch from Pedasa, most honored by Xerxes among his servants, who achieved singular vengeance against Panionius of Chios, the man who had castrated him as a boy and sold him into slavery.
per-talthybius: The legendary herald of Agamemnon whose anger, believed by Spartans to be divine, fell upon Lacedaemonians for killing Persian heralds at Sparta, a curse that persisted until it struck the descendants of the men sent to appease it.
per-midas: King of Phrygia, son of Gordias, famous for his great wealth and for dedicating his royal judgment seat as an offering at Delphi.
per-sadyattes: King of Lydia, son of Ardys, who ruled for twelve years and initiated the eleven-year war against Miletus before his son Alyattes continued it.
per-bias: Bias of Priene advised Croesus against building ships to attack the Greek islands and later counseled the Ionians to emigrate to Sardos to escape Persian domination.
per-agamemnon: Father of Orestes and Iphigenia, a legendary Greek king whose bones the Spartans sought on Apollo's oracle and whose daughter the Tauri believed they sacrificed.
per-ammon: An oracle in Libya consulted by Croesus and others, including the king Etearchus of the Ammonians, for divine pronouncements on Egyptian geography and other matters.
per-mandane: Daughter of Astyages, king of the Medes, married to the Persian Cambyses; her son Cyrus was ordered killed by her father after he dreamed her offspring would rule Asia in his place.
per-polynices: A legendary ancestor of Theras, included in the genealogy of the Spartan royal line descending through Thersander, Tisamenus, and Autesion.
per-sarpedon: Son of Europa, brother of Minos, driven from Crete and ruler of the Milyans in Asia (later called Lycians), after whom a headland in the Hellespont is named.
per-mazares: A Mede commanding Cyrus' forces in Lydia and Ionia after the fall of Sardis, tasked with enforcing Persian rule and pursuing the fugitive Pactyes until his death from illness.
per-arsames: Son of Darius and Artystone (daughter of Cyrus), commander of the Arabians and Ethiopians above Egypt in Xerxes' invasion force.
per-loxias: Apollo (god of prophecy at Delphi, called Loxias, who granted the Lydian king Croesus ambiguous oracles about war with Persia and whose oracle to the Cyrenean king Arcesilaus predicted the duration of his house's rule).
per-nitocris: An Assyrian queen and wife of Labynetus who made elaborate fortifications including canals diverting the Euphrates and a bridge connecting Babylon's two parts to protect her kingdom from Media.
per-epaphus: A sacred bull venerated by the Egyptians as a god, whom the Greeks identified with Epaphus, believed to be born miraculously and marked by specific physical signs including a white spot on the forehead and an eagle marking on the back.
per-hestia: A goddess worshipped by the Scythians (called Tabiti in their tongue) as their queen, and whose name the Greeks believed did not originate in Egypt.
per-linus: A figure in Egyptian mythology, son of Egypt's first king, after whose premature death the Linus-song (called Maneros in Egyptian) was composed as a dirge and became Egypt's earliest chant.
per-patarbemis: An Egyptian courtier of King Apries, sent to summon the rebel Amasis but mutilated by Apries upon his return, whereupon the Egyptian nobility abandoned Apries for Amasis.
per-typhon: In Egyptian mythology, a demon or hostile force whom the god Horus (identified by Herodotus with Apollo) deposed to become the last divine king of Egypt; also associated with a geographical location near the Serbonian marsh at Egypt's border.
per-iadmon: A Samian, son of Hephaestopolis, who owned both the courtesan Rhodopis and the fabulist Aesop as slaves.
per-inaros: A Libyan who rebelled against Persian rule in Egypt, slaying the Persian governor Achaemenes (Darius' son) at Papremis, though the Persians later honored his son Thannyras by restoring him to power.
per-psammis: King of Egypt, son of Necos, who reigned for six years and invaded Ethiopia before dying, after which his son Apries succeeded him.
per-ladice: A Greek woman from Cyrene, reportedly daughter of Battus, Arcesilaus, or Critobulus, married to Amasis of Egypt who initially suffered impotence with her until she vowed a statue to Aphrodite, after which he became fond of her and Cambyses later sent her safely back to Cyrene.
per-danaus: Ancestor of the Ionians and Khemmites, who according to Greek tradition traveled to Greece and was father or forebear of Perseus; the Khemmites claimed descent from him and his brother Lynceus through to Perseus, while his daughters were credited by Greeks with bringing the Thesmophoria rite from Egypt to the Pelasgian women.
per-octamasades: King of the Scythians, son of the daughter of Teres, who replaced his brother Scyles and executed him for adopting foreign customs.
per-mandrocles: Samian engineer who designed the pontoon bridge that Darius used to cross the Bosporus during his Scythian campaign, and who was rewarded by the king with gifts and honors.
per-idanthyrsus: King of the greater division of the Scythian royal people who led the resistance against Darius' Persian invasion by executing a strategy of retreat and scorched-earth tactics.
per-charilaus: Brother of the tyrant Maeandrius of Samos, imprisoned for unspecified offense; he persuaded Maeandrius to attack the Persian forces occupying the island, leading an armed assault on the Persians that briefly succeeded before being overwhelmed by reinforcements.
per-laius: A legendary king of Thebes, son of Labdacus and father of Oedipus, invoked in oracular instruction and used by Herodotus to date ancient dedications at Thebes.
per-eurysthenes: One of the two sons of Aristodemus who became kings of Sparta, founder of the royal house bearing his name.
per-corobius: A Cretan murex fisherman from Itanus who had been blown off course to Libya and guided Theraean colonists to the island of Platea, where he was later resupplied by Samian sailors.
per-sataspes: An Achaemenid Persian of royal blood (nephew of Darius, son of Teaspes) who was condemned to death by Xerxes for rape but given the alternative punishment of circumnavigating Libya; he sailed beyond the Pillars of Heracles and southward along the African coast but turned back after months at sea, claiming the ship could proceed no farther, and was executed by Xerx
per-jason: A legendary Greek hero who commanded the Argo in its voyage to Colchis and later, according to mythological accounts, sailed around the Peloponnese and encountered Triton in Libya.
per-daurises: A Persian general married to a daughter of Darius, who pursued Ionians to Sardis, conquered cities of the Hellespont, and was killed in an ambush at Pedasus during the Ionian Revolt while marching against the Carians.
per-crius: An Aeginetan aristocrat and son of Polycritus who opposed King Cleomenes' arrest of Aeginetans in 491 BC, later taken hostage to Athens, and whose son Polycritus distinguished himself in the naval battle at Salamis.
per-marsyas: A river in Caria that flows from Idria into the Maeander, and the site where Carians fought Persians under Daurises; also the name of a Silenus whose skin, according to Phrygian tradition, was flayed by Apollo and hung at Celaenae in Phrygia.
per-labda: Mother of Cypselus the Corinthian tyrant; a crippled daughter of the Bacchiad oligarch Amphion who married the Lapith Eetion and, warned by an oracle's fulfilment, hid her newborn son from ten assassins sent by the Bacchiadae to kill him.
per-callimachus: Polemarch of Athens whose casting vote decided the Athenians to fight at Marathon; he commanded the right wing and was killed in the battle.
per-anaxilaus: Tyrant of Rhegium who allied with the Samians to seize Zancle, and whose son-in-law status (through marriage to Cydippe) connected him to the Carthaginian expedition against Sicily led by Amilcas.
per-agetus: A Spartan, friend of King Ariston, whose wife Ariston seduced through a oath-bound wager and took as his third wife.
per-tigranes: Commander of the Median contingent in Xerxes' invasion army, and later general of the Persian land force at Mykale, where he was killed in battle against the Greeks; described as the noblest and tallest man in Persia.
per-sophanes: An Athenian from Decelea who killed the Argive pentathlete Eurybates in single combat during the siege of Aegina and later died as general fighting the Edonians at Datus over gold-mines.
per-pharnaces: Father of Artabazus; a Persian of high standing in Xerxes' court whose son commanded forces in the invasion of Greece and later withdrew from the Battle of Plataea.
per-pytheas: Son of Ischenous, an Aeginetan hoplite who fought heroically against the Persians at Salamis and was so severely wounded that the Persian soldiers preserved his life in admiration of his valor, later rescued when a Sidonian ship carrying him was captured by Polycritus.
per-telines: An ancestor of Gelon of Gela who, through his use of sacred religious instruments of the goddesses of the underworld, restored exiled Geloans to their city and thereby established his descendants as hereditary priests of these goddesses.
per-bacis: A Greek prophet or oracle-giver whose oracles concerning the Persian Wars—including predictions about Euboea, Salamis, and Plataea—Herodotus treats as genuinely prophetic and fulfilled.
per-amilcas: King of Carthage, son of Hanno, who led a massive force of North African and Mediterranean peoples against Sicily to support Terillus but was defeated by Gelon and Theron in battle, reportedly perishing in the flames of his own sacrificial pyre.
per-megistias: A seer of Acarnanian birth descended from Melampus who predicted the Greeks' doom at Thermopylae from sacrificial omens and, despite being dismissed by Leonidas, remained and died with the Spartan forces.
per-europa: Daughter of a Phoenician king, abducted by Greeks to Crete; eponym (according to Herodotus) of the continent Europe, though she never traveled beyond Phoenicia, Crete, and Lycia.
per-myrsus: A Lydian, son of Gyges, who served as messenger for the Persian Oroetes to Polycrates of Samos and later died fighting the Carians as a Persian general.
per-adeimantus: Corinthian general who initially opposed Themistocles' tactical advice before Salamis but reportedly fled the battle in panic, later returning when persuaded by a mysterious boat that the Greeks were winning.
per-lampon: A leading man of Aegina who urged Pausanias after Plataea to mutilate Mardonius' corpse in revenge for Leonidas, but was rebuked and dismissed.
per-medea: Daughter of the Colchian king, carried off by Greek heroes sailing to Aea; her abduction was cited by the Trojans as precedent for Paris' seizure of Helen, and her arrival among the Arians caused them to change their name to Medes.
per-alcaeus: The passage in 1.7 references Alcaeus as an ancestor in a genealogy (son of Heracles, grandfather of Agron), establishing the Heraclid dynasty of Lydia; the passage in 5.95 refers to Alcaeus the poet of Mytilene, whose armor was captured by Athenians at Sigeum during a war between Mytilene and Athens.
per-tellus: An Athenian whom Solon named the most fortunate of men, distinguished by his prosperous life, virtuous children, and glorious death in battle against Eleusis fighting for Athens.
per-alilat: A goddess identified with the heavenly Aphrodite, worshipped by Arabians and associated with Assyrian Mylitta and Persian Mitra.
per-gordias: Father of Midas and grandfather of Adrastus; a king of Phrygia whose lineage marked the royal house from which Adrastus descended.
per-phraortes: A Median king, son of Deioces, who conquered the Persians and other Asian nations before perishing in war against the Assyrians after a reign of twenty-two years.
per-codrus: The legendary king of Athens whose name was invoked to date the first Dorian settlement at Megara, and ancestor of the Pisistratid dynasty through his descendants Melanthus and subsequent rulers.
per-leon: Co-king of Sparta with Hegesicles, under whom the Spartans defeated the Tegeans in war though earlier campaigns had failed.
per-tabalus: A Persian governor appointed by Cyrus to administer Sardis after its conquest, besieged in the acropolis by the revolting Lydian Pactyes until relieved by Mazares.
per-lycus: An Athenian who migrated to Asia Minor and gave his name to the Lycians, after joining Sarpedon in the land of the Termilae.
per-min: The first king of Egypt, who separated Memphis from the Nile by constructing a dam that redirected the river's flow and founded the city of Memphis.
per-oedipus: A figure from Greek myth, son of Laius, whose avenging spirits received a temple cult by the Aegidae clan of Sparta to ensure the survival of their children.
per-cassandane: Mother of Cambyses and wife of Cyrus the Great; daughter of Pharnaspes, an Achaemenid; her death was mourned by Cyrus and his subjects, and her son allegedly vowed as a child to conquer Egypt after she complained of Cyrus' favor toward an Egyptian concubine.
per-arkhandrus: A legendary Achaean hero, son of Phthius and son-in-law of Danaus, after whom a town in the Egyptian Delta was named.
per-mendes: An Egyptian district whose inhabitants held sacred goats (particularly he-goats) and worshipped Pan, in contrast to the Theban district which worshipped Zeus and held rams sacred.
per-amyrtaeus: An Egyptian king whose son, Pausiris, was restored to power by the Persians after Amyrtaeus himself had revolted against them and caused them great harm.
per-tyndarus: Father of Helen and Castor and Pollux (the Dioscuri), legendary king of Sparta whose sons aided in recovering their sister from Attica.
per-dioscuri: The Dioscuri were divine brothers (Castor and Pollux) known to Greeks as patrons of seafarers, whom Egyptians did not include among their gods and who were named by the Pelasgians rather than derived from Egypt.
per-archias: A Lacedaemonian hoplite who entered the fortress at Samos with fleeing residents during the Spartan campaign and was killed there fighting.
per-aspathines: A Persian of highest rank, one of the seven conspirators against the Magi who wounded one Magus in the thigh during their rebellion, and father of Prexaspes the naval commander.
per-lycophron: Younger son of Periander of Corinth, who refused to speak to his father after learning that Periander had killed his mother Melissa, and was eventually murdered by the Corcyraeans to prevent his father's arrival in their city.
per-artystone: Daughter of Cyrus and wife of Darius, whom Darius especially loved and by whom he fathered Arsames and Gobryas.
per-arge: One of two Hyperborean maidens (with Opis) who came to Delos with the gods themselves and received honors, gifts, and hymns from the Delians.
per-ariapithes: A king of Scythia, father of Scyles, whose deputy Tymnes provided information to Herodotus about Anacharsis' lineage.
per-scylax: A navigator from Caryanda whom Darius sent to sail down the Indus River to discover where it emptied into the sea; also a ship captain from Myndus serving under Megabates in the Ionian expedition against Naxos, whom Megabates brutally punished for negligent watch-keeping.
per-aeschylus: An Athenian tragedian, son of Euphorion, whom Herodotus credits with originating the notion that Artemis was daughter of Demeter.
per-pythagoras: A Greek philosopher of Samos, master of the slave Salmoxis, remembered as one of the greatest Greek teachers.
per-laodamas: Laodamas of Phocaea, one of the Ionian rulers who opposed Miltiades' plan to destroy the bridge over the Ister.
per-pallas: Pallas is a name for Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare, invoked in dedications and oracles concerning Athens.
per-coes: A citizen of Mytilene whom Darius rewarded for counsel by making tyrant of his city, but who was stoned to death by the Mytilenaeans when Aristagoras deposed the tyrants during the Ionian Revolt.
per-philippus: A noble Greek from Croton, Olympic victor and notably handsome, who accompanied the explorer Dorieus to Libya and was killed there; after his death, the Egestans honored him with a hero shrine and sacrifices.
per-anchimolius: A Spartan commander sent by the Lacedaemonians to expel the Pisistratidae from Athens, killed in battle at Phalerum when Thessalian cavalry routed his army.
per-tisandrus: Father of the Athenian suitor Hippocleides, who competed for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-bacchiadae: An oligarchic clan that ruled Corinth, who received oracles predicting that the offspring of one of their members would overthrow their power, and sent men to kill the child but failed when none could bring themselves to commit the murder.
per-socles: A Corinthian envoy who persuades the allies of Sparta to oppose their plan to restore the tyrant Hippias to Athens.
per-erechtheus: An ancient king of Athens after whom the Athenians took their name Athenians, father of Orithyia (whom Boreas married), and associated with a shrine on the Athenian acropolis containing an olive tree and salt pool.
per-zeuxidemus: Son of Leutychides, king of Sparta; he died before his father and never reached the kingship, leaving his son Archidemus.
per-chersis: Chersis was a king of Salamis in Cyprus, grandfather of Onesilus and Gorgus, and father of Philaon.
per-philippides: An Athenian herald and long-distance runner sent by the generals to Sparta during the Persian Wars, famous for his reported encounter with Pan on Mount Parthenion.
per-nicodromus: An exiled Aeginetan nobleman who conspired with the Athenians to betray Aegina, seized the Old City as agreed, but escaped when Athenian aid arrived late.
per-agariste: Daughter of Cleisthenes, tyrant of Sicyon, betrothed to Megacles son of Alcmeon of Athens in a famous contest of suitors, and mother of the reformer Cleisthenes who established Athenian democracy.
per-aleuadae: Thessalian aristocratic family whose princes invited Xerxes to invade Greece and persuaded him to undertake the expedition, though the wider Thessalian population resisted their pro-Persian policy.
per-ariphron: Father of Xanthippus and grandfather of Pericles; an Athenian of the prominent Alcmeonid family.
per-athamas: A figure from Greek mythology, son of Aeolus, whose story of attempted murder (plotted with Ino against Phrixus) and subsequent scapegoating was commemorated in Achaean religious practice that Xerxes observed during his campaign.
per-teispes: Ancestor of Xerxes, appearing in the Persian royal genealogy traced back through Darius and Cyrus.
per-musaeus: An ancient Greek diviner and prophet whose oracles were collected and edited by Onomacritus and selectively recited to encourage Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
per-athena-pronaea: A goddess worshipped at Delphi whose temple witnessed miraculous phenomena—falling rocks from Parnassus and divine thunderbolts—that repelled the Persian barbarians during their advance toward the sanctuary.
per-cleandrus: Tyrant of Gela, slain by Sabyllus after ruling seven years; brother of Hippocrates.
per-mascames: Governor of Doriscus appointed by Xerxes, who earned such distinction for his valor that Persian kings sent him annual gifts and subsequently honored his descendants.
per-sandoces: Viceroy from Cyme in Aeolia and captain of fifteen Persian ships at Artemisium, who had previously been crucified and pardoned by Darius for bribery, but was captured by Greeks when his separated squadron mistook them for the Persian fleet.
per-phylacus: A Samian, son of Histiaeus, who captured Hellenic ships at Salamis and was rewarded by the Persian king with land and the title of orosangas (benefactor); distinct from the hero Phylacus of Delphi.
per-attaginus: A Theban notable who hosted Mardonius and his Persian officers at a banquet before Plataea, subsequently demanded by the Greeks after the battle but who escaped before surrendering to Pausanias.
per-aristides: Athenian general at Salamis and Plataea; though previously ostracized, he warned of the Persian encirclement before the battle and was recognized as the most just man in Athens.
per-lycidas: An Athenian councillor who advocated accepting Mardonius' peace offer during the Persian Wars, subsequently stoned to death by the Athenian people for his proposal.
per-euryanax: A Spartan of the same family as Pausanias, chosen as his colleague in command of the five thousand Spartans marching against the Persians at Plataea.
per-eurystheus: A king of the Peloponnese, whose death preceded the Heraclidae's attempted return to the Peloponnese, which was thwarted when the Tegean champion Echemus killed Hyllus in single combat.
per-ardys: King of Lydia, son of Gyges, who reigned forty-nine years and conquered Priene while the Cimmerians took Sardis during his reign.
per-murychides: A man from the Hellespont sent by Mardonius to Salamis to offer peace terms to the Athenians during their retreat in 479 BC, whom the Athenians permitted to depart safely after stoning to death the councillor Lycidas who had favored the proposal.
per-lydus: Eponymous founder of Lydia, son of Atys, from whom the Lydian region and people derived their name.
per-chilon: A Spartan sage whose warning about the vulnerability of Cythera to attack became proverbial among Laconians, and who counseled Hippocrates against fathering Pisistratus.
per-lygdamis: A tyrant of Naxos who supported Pisistratus' return to power in Athens with money and troops, and was subsequently placed in charge of Naxos after its conquest.
per-ismenian-apollo: A sanctuary at Thebes in Boeotia sacred to Apollo, where divination occurred through sacrifice and where Herodotus saw dedications including golden offerings from Croesus and inscribed tripods from antiquity.
per-orestes: The legendary son of Agamemnon whose bones, according to a Delphic oracle, the Spartans sought and recovered from Tegea to gain military superiority over the Tegeans.
per-lichas: A Spartan "doer of good deeds" (an honorably retired knight) who discovered the tomb of Orestes near Tegea through conversation with a blacksmith, enabling Sparta's military ascendancy in the Peloponnese.
per-othryades: A Lacedaemonian hoplite, sole survivor of three hundred champions sent to fight the Argives for control of Thyreae, who stripped the enemy dead and held his ground but subsequently took his own life from shame at being the only survivor.
per-syennesis: King of Cilicia who reconciled the warring Lydians and Medes by arranging a marriage compact between them, and whose daughter married Pixodarus of Cindya; a Cilician commander in Xerxes' navy during the invasion of Greece.
per-mylitta: A goddess known to the Assyrians by this name, identified by Herodotus as the Persian "heavenly" Aphrodite, to whom men invoke her name during a sacred prostitution ritual in Babylon.
per-eteocles: Father of Laodamas and a ruler of the Cadmeans whose reign preceded the expulsion of that people by the Argives.
per-labynetus: Ruler of Babylon who, with Syennesis of Cilicia, negotiated peace between the Lydians and Medes in the sixth year of their conflict, and later maintained an alliance with Croesus against Cyrus; his son, also named Labynetus, inherited the sovereignty of Assyria and was conquered by Cyrus.
per-pantaleon: A son of Alyattes and half-brother of Croesus (by an Ionian mother), who led a faction against Croesus before his kingship and conspired to seize the throne of Lydia, but was defeated when Croesus gained sovereignty.
per-heraclides: Father of Aristagoras of Cyme, a tyrant who led the Ionian Revolt against Persian rule.
per-spargapises: Son of Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae, leader of their forces; captured by Cyrus after being ambushed at a banquet, he killed himself after being freed from his bonds.
per-pharnaspes: Father of Cassandane, who married Cyrus and bore Cambyses, making Pharnaspes grandfather of the Persian king Cambyses.
per-maneros: The only son of Egypt's first king, who died prematurely and was commemorated by a dirge that became the Egyptians' earliest chant.
per-tritantaechmes: Governor of Babylon under the Persian king, son of Artabazus, whose enormous wealth and resources exemplified the province's vast power; later served as a general commanding a division of Xerxes' land army during the invasion of Greece.
per-hesiod: Ancient Greek poet who, along with Homer, established the genealogy and attributes of the gods for the Greeks.
per-memnon: A figure in mythology, often confused with the colossal rock statues of Sesostris in Ionia, though Herodotus dismisses this identification as incorrect, and a place-name on the royal road from Sardis to Susa.
per-nereids: Sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus, to whom Persian Magi made ritual offerings to calm a storm at Sepia during Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
per-busiris: A town in the middle of the Egyptian Delta, site of a major temple of Isis where Egyptians gathered for sacred festivals and rituals.
per-pheros: An Egyptian king, son and successor of Sesostris, who became blind after hurling a spear into the Nile's flood and regained his sight through the urine of a faithful woman, whom he then married, while burning all other women he had tested; he erected two massive stone obelisks in the temple of the Sun as an offering for his recovery.
per-khephren: An Egyptian pharaoh and brother of Kheops who built a smaller pyramid at Giza, reportedly reigning fifty-six years.
per-rhampsinitus: An Egyptian king of the Old Kingdom, successor to Proteus, remembered for building statues at the temple of Hephaestus and for the legend of his descent to Hades, which the Egyptians commemorated with an annual festival.
per-aesop: A writer of fables who was a slave of Iadmon the Samian and a fellow-slave of the courtesan Rhodopis, killed at Delphi.
per-euphorion: Euphorion was an Arcadian whose family according to local tradition kept open house after entertaining the Dioscuri, and father of the suitor Laphanes.
per-gillus: An exile from Tarentum who rescued Persian shipwrecked sailors on the Iapygian coast and asked King Darius to restore him to his homeland, though the Cnidians' attempt to return him to Tarentum ultimately failed.
per-pindar: Pindar was a Greek lyric poet whose maxim that "custom is lord of all" Herodotus cites as authoritative support for his theory about universal human attachment to native customs.
per-phaedyme: Daughter of Otanes and wife of Cambyses; she discovered the impostor Magus Smerdis lacked ears, confirming he was not the true Smerdis son of Cyrus.
per-thonis: Warden of the Nile mouth at the Canopic mouth who, upon learning from suppliants that Paris had abducted Helen, reported the matter to Proteus and arrested Paris and his ships.
per-penelope: In Greek mythology, the mother of Pan (by Hermes, according to Greek tradition) and wife of Odysseus whose name Herodotus cites when establishing the chronology of Pan's existence relative to the Trojan War.
per-sabacos: King of Ethiopia who invaded and ruled Egypt for fifty years, establishing a just rule based on labor rather than execution, before voluntarily departing after a prophetic dream indicated his allotted time had ended.
per-lycaretus: Brother of Maeandrius who ruled Samos; after murdering imprisoned citizens to seize power, he was later appointed Persian governor of Lemnos, where he was killed for attempting to enslave the population.
per-gelonus: Gelonus was the second son of Heracles and the serpent-woman in Scythian mythology, who was cast out by his mother for failing to fulfill the requirements of his father's test, and his name was also borne by a wooden city of Greek origin inhabited by the Geloni among the Budini in Scythia.
per-targitaus: Legendary founder of the Scythian people, said to be son of Zeus and a river-nymph, whose three sons ruled Scythia and whose line held the sacred golden implements that fell from heaven.
per-achilles: A hero whose name was given to a Scythian racecourse-shaped region (the Racecourse of Achilles) near the Hypacuris river and the Woodland.
per-saulius: A Scythian king who killed his brother Anacharsis for adopting Greek religious practices.
per-tymnes: Deputy (proxenos) for the Scythian king Ariapithes, from whom Herodotus learned that Anacharsis was uncle of King Idanthyrsus and son of Gnurus.
per-artanes: A Persian, brother of King Darius I and son of Hystaspes, whose daughter Phratagune married Darius and received her father's entire estate as dowry.
per-phronime: Daughter of Etearchus, ruler of Oaxus in Crete, mistreated by her stepmother, cast into the sea by a Theraean trader on her father's orders, rescued and brought to Thera where she became concubine of Polymnestus and mother of Battus, founder of Cyrene.
per-grinnus: King of Thera, descendant of Theras, who received an oracle at Delphi commanding him to found a city in Libya but delegated the task to the younger Battus, setting in motion the eventual colonization of Cyrene.
per-membliarus: A Phoenician, son of Poeciles and relative of Cadmus, left on the island of Calliste (later Thera) by Cadmus during his search for Europa, where his descendants dwelt for eight generations before Theras arrived from Lacedaemon to settle among them.
per-agenor: Father of Cadmus and Cilix; a Phoenician whose sons feature in legends of early Mediterranean settlement and migration.
per-evelthon: A king of Salamis in Cyprus who refused to grant military aid to Pheretime, mother of the Cyrenean prince Arcesilaus, and dedicated a celebrated censer at Delphi.
per-bubares: A Persian general who married Alexander of Macedon's sister Gygaea to suppress the search for Persian envoys killed by Alexander, and later oversaw the digging of the canal through the Athos isthmus under Xerxes' invasion preparations.
per-sisamnes: A Persian royal judge under Cambyses, executed and flayed for accepting a bribe, his skin used to cover the seat where his son and successor Otanes then judged.
per-alazir: King of the Barcaeans, father-in-law of Arcesilaus of Cyrene, killed alongside Arcesilaus by men of Barce and Cyrenean exiles.
per-telys: Tyrant of Sybaris who prepared to march against Croton and whose daughter was betrothed to Philippus of Croton before he was banished.
per-ephors: Five magistrates elected by the Spartan assembly who wielded executive and judicial authority, including the power to summon and reprimand even the kings; they enforced the laws of Sparta and acted as guardians of the state's traditional order.
per-gorgo: Daughter of Cleomenes and wife of Leonidas, king of Sparta; she discovered the secret message about Xerxes' invasion plans hidden in a waxed tablet.
per-harmodius: An Athenian of Gephyraean descent who, with Aristogeiton, slew the tyrant Hipparchus son of Pisistratus, becoming celebrated as a liberator of Athens though later sources questioned whether he and his partner truly ended the tyranny.
per-badres: Admiral of the Persian fleet sent by Aryandes to help Pheretime against Barce, and later commander of various Asian contingents in Xerxes' invasion force.
per-auxesia: A goddess whose wooden images, made from Athenian olive wood and set up in Epidaurus on the Delphic priestess's instructions, were later stolen by the Aeginetans and enshrined at Oea.
per-pisistratid: A dynastic ruling family of Athens who controlled the city for thirty-six years until their expulsion by Lacedaemonian intervention around 510 BC, after which they settled at Sigeum in the Troad.
per-simonides: A lyric poet of Ceos who commemorated the death of the seer Megistias at Thermopylae through an inscription, and who earlier praised the Eretrian general Eualcides.
per-damia: A fertility goddess (with Auxesia) whose olive-wood image, made for Epidaurus at Delphi's bidding, was stolen by the Aeginetans and honored with abusive female choruses.
per-hymaees: A Persian general, son-in-law of Darius, who pursued Ionians after their attack on Sardis and subsequently conquered cities in the Propontis and Aeolia before dying of illness in the Troad.
per-ajax: A legendary Greek hero, son of Telamon, invoked as a divine ally by the Greeks at Salamis and honored with a Phoenician trireme dedicated at Salamis after the Persian Wars.
per-hermippus: A man of Atarneus who intercepted letters from Histiaeus intended for Persian conspirators and delivered them instead to Artaphrenes, thereby exposing the revolt plot.
per-acrisius: Grandfather of Perseus (through his daughter Danae); cited in genealogical discussions of Dorian kingship, his ancestry traced back to Egypt according to Greek tradition.
per-aristomachus: Ancestor of the Spartan royal houses, son of Cleodaeus and father of Aristodemus, from whom both the Eurypontid and Agiad lines descended.
per-cobon: A Delphian of great influence, son of Aristophantus, who was bribed by Cleomenes to persuade the Pythia to falsely declare Demaratus not the son of Ariston, and was subsequently exiled from Delphi when the conspiracy was exposed.
per-cleodaeus: Ancestor of the Spartan royal houses, son of Hyllus and father of Aristomachus in the genealogy descending from Heracles.
per-dionysius: A Phocaean general who attempted to train the Ionian fleet at Lade for battle against Xerxes' forces but, after the Ionians mutinied and abandoned his discipline, fled to Sicily where he became a pirate preying on Phoenicians and Etruscans.
per-eurybates: An Argive pentathlon champion who led a thousand volunteers to Aegina's aid and was killed in single combat by the Athenian Sophanes during the Athenian siege of Aegina.
per-argus: A sanctuary of the god Argus near Argos where Argive refugees took shelter after their defeat by Cleomenes and the Spartans, subsequently burned by Cleomenes in defiance of its sacred status.
per-menares: Father of Leotychides, a Spartan king of the second royal house; appears in genealogies establishing Leotychides' lineage from Heracles.
per-artaxerxes: Son of Xerxes and king of Persia, whose reign followed his father's unsuccessful invasion of Greece; known to the Greeks as "the Great Warrior."
per-archidemus: Son of Zeuxidemus and grandson of Leutychides, a Spartan royal of the line that produced kings; he married Lampito, daughter of Leutychides.
per-timo: A Parian under-priestess of Demeter who advised Miltiades during his failed siege of Paros, but was later absolved by the Delphic oracle of blame for guiding him.
per-pelops: A legendary Phrygian ruler whom Persian tradition claims subjugated Greece so thoroughly that the land and people bear his name.
per-perses: A legendary ancestor of the Persians, son of Perseus and Andromeda, from whom the Persians derived their name.
per-cepheus: King of Ethiopia, father of Andromeda, from whom the Persians claimed descent through his daughter's marriage to Perseus.
per-artobazanes: Eldest son of Darius by his first wife (daughter of Gobryas), who contested with his half-brother Xerxes for succession to the Persian throne but was passed over when Darius declared Xerxes king instead.
per-mardontes: A Persian commander of the island tribes in Xerxes' invasion fleet, appointed as admiral at Samos after Salamis, killed fighting at Mykale.
per-pharnuches: A Persian cavalry captain under Xerxes who fell ill and was left behind at Sardis, then lost his command after his horse threw him and he began vomiting blood and wasting away.
per-xuthus: A mythical ancestor of the Ionians, whose son Ion gave his name to the Ionian people.
per-boges: Persian governor of Eion who, when besieged by the Athenians under Cimon, chose death and destruction of his household over surrender, earning lasting Persian praise for his loyalty.
per-aneristus: Father of Sperthias, a Spartan nobleman who volunteered to atone for the death of Persian heralds killed at Sparta.
per-ariabignes: Admiral of the Ionian and Carian fleet under Xerxes, son of Darius and brother of Xerxes, killed at the Battle of Salamis.
per-adimantus: A Corinthian admiral whose ship received three talents of silver from Themistocles at Artemisium to prevent the Greek fleet from withdrawing during the Persian Wars.
per-bulis: A Spartan noble of great wealth, son of Nicolaus, who voluntarily offered himself for execution at Xerxes' court to atone for the Spartan killing of the Persian king's heralds.
per-neocles: Father of the Athenian general Themistocles, mentioned only in patronymic references to his son's role in the Persian Wars.
per-sperthias: A Spartan of noble birth and wealth who volunteered to go to Xerxes' court to atone for Sparta's killing of Persian heralds, and later his son Aneristus was captured and executed by the Athenians as divine punishment for the original offense.
per-syagrus: A Lacedaemonian envoy sent to Sicily to negotiate with Gelon, who angrily insists on Spartan command of the Greek forces against the Persians and rejects Gelon's offer of compromise.
per-artoxerxes: Son of Xerxes and king of Persia, who confirmed to Argive envoys that their friendship with the Persian throne remained intact.
per-cecrops: Founder and early king of Athens, eponymous ancestor of the Cecropidae; referenced in oracles concerning Persian invasion and Athenian resistance.
per-leontiades: Theban general at Thermopylae who led the Theban contingent under Leonidas but defected to Xerxes' side during the battle, later being branded by the Persian king's order.
per-terillus: Tyrant of Himera who, after being expelled by Theron of Acragas, allied with the Carthaginian king Amilcas against Sicily and prevented Gelon from aiding the Greeks at Delphi.
per-tellias: A diviner from Elis who devised a stratagem for the Phocians besieged on Parnassus, covering six hundred warriors with gypsum to rout the Thessalian army by night.
per-onetes: A Carystian whom some claimed guided the Persians around Mt. Oeta during the invasion of Greece, but Herodotus rejects this account in favor of Epialtes the Trachinian as the actual guide.
per-dicaeus: An Athenian exile in the Persian court who witnesses a divine portent near Eleusis during Xerxes' invasion and interprets it as an omen of the Persian fleet's destruction at Salamis.
per-phrixus: Son of Athamas and Ino in Greek mythology, whose descendants were subject to ritual sacrifice in Achaea according to an oracle, until Cytissorus his son rescued Athamas from sacrifice and drew divine wrath upon his own line.
per-theomestor: Samian tyrant installed by the Persians after he captured Hellenic ships at the battle of Salamis, whom the islanders later worked to undermine during the campaign at Mykale.
per-doris: A region in central Greece between Malian and Phocian territory, the ancient homeland of the Peloponnesian Dorians, which the Persian army passed through without harm during Xerxes' invasion because its inhabitants supported the Persians.
per-lysimachus: Aristides son of Lysimachus, the just, was an Athenian statesman who, though once ostracized, fought at Salamis and commanded the Athenians at Plataea.
per-eleusinian-demeter: A goddess venerated at Plataea and Mykale with sanctuaries marking both battle sites where Greeks defeated Persian forces.
per-sicinnus: Themistocles' trusted servant who carried secret messages to the Persian commanders at Salamis and later to Xerxes, and whom Themistocles subsequently enrolled as a Thespian citizen and enriched.
per-mermnadae: The royal dynasty that ruled Sardis and Lydia after overthrowing the Heraclidae, beginning with Gyges who made extensive offerings at Delphi.
per-aeropus: One of three brothers of Temenid descent who came from Argos to Macedonia, where he served as a thete in the household of a Macedonian king; ancestor of the royal line through his son Alcetes.
per-posidonius: A Spartan "iren" (senior warrior) judged the bravest at Plataea for his courageous fighting without seeking death, killed in the battle and honored in a tomb there.
per-biton: An Argive youth of exceptional strength who, with his brother Cleobis, pulled his mother's wagon to the temple of Hera and died peacefully in the temple thereafter, held up by Solon as an example of a blessed life.
per-cleobis: An Argive youth of great strength who, together with his brother Biton, drew his mother's wagon to Hera's temple and was cited by Solon as an example of human happiness, dying peacefully in the temple afterward.
per-agron: First Heraclid king of Sardis, son of Ninus, and ancestor of the Mermnad dynasty that ruled Lydia until Candaules.
per-deiphonus: A diviner from Apollonia (in the Ionian gulf), son of Evenius, who provided favorable omens for the Greeks at Samos before the battle of Mycale, though some sources claim he falsely used Evenius' name and was a hired prophet.
per-theodorus: A Samian artisan renowned for fine metalwork, credited with crafting a large silver mixing-bowl dedicated to Delphi by Croesus and a seal-ring set in emerald for Polycrates.
