per-trophonius: A hero and oracle-site in Boeotia (Lebadea), to which Croesus sent inquiries and which Xerxes' agent Mys consulted by bribing a local to descend into the sacred cave.
per-callicrates: A Spartan "iren" (elite warrior) renowned for his exceptional beauty and valor, killed by an arrow while sitting near Pausanias during the Battle of Plataea, mourning that he died without striking a blow for Greece.
per-deucalion: A legendary king in whose reign the Hellenic people inhabited the land of Phthia before their subsequent migrations.
per-amphilytus: An Acarnanian diviner who met Pisistratus near the temple of Pallenian Athena and prophesied his victory in hexameter verse before his battle against the Athenians.
per-hyroeades: A Mardian soldier in Cyrus's army who first scaled the supposedly unassailable acropolis of Sardis by discovering an unguarded path, enabling its capture from Croesus.
per-sandanis: A Lydian wise man who advised King Croesus against invading Persia, warning that the Persians' austere way of life made them formidable and that conquest would bring Lydia no benefit.
per-cyno: The wife of Mitradates, Astyages' cowherd; she raised the infant Cyrus in the mountains of Media and became known in Persian legend as the nurse who saved him.
per-meles: Former king of Sardis who failed to carry a sacred lion around the entire acropolis wall, leaving one sheer side unguarded and thus enabling the Persian capture of the city.
per-mitradates: A Median cowherd in the service of Astyages who, with his wife Spako, raised the infant Cyrus after being ordered to expose him in the mountains.
per-cybele: A goddess of Phrygia, worshipped at Sardis, whose temple was burned during the Persian siege and subsequently invoked by Persians as justification for destroying Greek temples.
per-athena-alea: A goddess worshipped at Tegea in Arcadia, where the Lacedaemonians dedicated spoils of war including chains from their defeat by the Tegeans and a bronze feeding trough of Mardonius taken after Plataea.
per-melanthus: An early king of Athens, legendary ancestor of the Pisistratid dynasty through his descent to Codrus.
per-pandion: An Athenian whose son Lycus migrated to Asia Minor and gave his name to the Lycian people.
per-anacreon: A lyric poet of Teos who was in the company of Polycrates of Samos when an envoy from the Persian satrap Oroetes arrived.
per-timesius: An early colonist from Clazomenae who founded Abdera in Thrace but was expelled by the Thracians, and subsequently received heroic honors from the Teians who resettled the city.
per-arganthonius: King of Tartessus in the far west who befriended Phocaean Greeks, ruled eighty years and lived to one hundred twenty, and gave them money to wall their city upon learning of growing Median power.
per-aegeus: King of Athens who banished his brother Lycus, mentioned in the context of early Cretan and Lycian history.
per-semiramis: A legendary queen of Babylon who built dikes to control the plain's flooding, regarded as a notable builder of the city five generations before Herodotus' own time.
per-alcmene: Mother of Heracles (son of Amphitryon), said by Herodotus to be Egyptian by descent, though she was known to Greeks as the wife of Amphitryon.
per-sappho: Sister of Kharaxus of Mytilene, a poetess whose brother is criticized in her poetry for freeing the courtesan Rhodopis in Egypt.
per-melkart:
Melkart is not explicitly named in these passages; the references are to "Heracles" as worshipped by Phoenicians at Tyre and elsewhere, whom Greek sources identify with their own Heracles, but Herodotus does not use the Phoenician name Melkart.

UNKNOWN
per-horus: In Egyptian mythology, the son of Osiris who deposed Typhon and was the last divine king of Egypt before human rulers, identified by Herodotus with the Greek Apollo.
per-kharaxus: A man of Mytilene, son of Scamandronymus and brother of the poet Sappho, who freed the courtesan Rhodopis in Egypt and was subsequently criticized by his sister in her poetry.
per-hector: Hector was the eldest son of Priam, king of Troy, and heir to the throne, who according to Herodotus should have compelled his brother Alexandrus to return Helen to the Greeks but did not.
per-asukhis: A king of Egypt who succeeded Mycerinus and built the eastern court of Hephaestus' temple, instituted a law allowing loans secured by fathers' corpses, and constructed a brick pyramid.
per-semele: Semele, daughter of Cadmus in Greek tradition, mother of Dionysus; Herodotus dates this Dionysus to approximately 1600 years before his own time.
per-nitetis: Daughter of the deposed Egyptian king Apries, sent by Amasis (disguised as his own daughter) to Cambyses as a concubine, whose revelation of her true identity provoked his invasion of Egypt.
per-critobulus: A citizen of Cyrene, possibly the father of Ladice who married Amasis of Egypt.
per-orotalt: A name for Dionysus among the Arabian peoples, whom Herodotus identifies as equivalent to the Greek god in their religious practice.
per-patizeithes: A Magus, steward of Cambyses' household, who orchestrated the rebellion of his brother (also named Smerdis) by impersonating the deceased son of Cyrus and placing him on the throne.
per-king-cambyses: Son of Cyrus II, Persian king who conquered Egypt; his reign is marked by the false Smerdis affair and conflict with rebellious Magi.
per-samius: Father of an Archias; named Samius because his son Archias died fighting bravely at Samos and was publicly buried there.
per-aristophilides: King of Tarentum in Italy who detained Persian envoys and their ship to aid the escape of the Greek physician Democedes.
per-parmys: Daughter of Cyrus' son Smerdis, married by Darius I, and mother of Ariomardus, who commanded the Moschi and Tibareni in Xerxes' invasion army.
per-lipoxais: Eldest son of Targitaïs in Scythian myth, father of the Auchatae clan.
per-helios: The sun god, invoked in Polycrates' daughter's prophetic dream as the agent who would anoint her father's crucified body with his sweat.
per-amphilochus: A legendary Greek hero, son of Amphiaraus, who founded Posideion on the Cilician-Syrian border and whose descendants, the Pamphylians, provided ships for Xerxes' invasion fleet.
per-artontes: Father of Bagaeus, a Persian who served King Darius; also father of Mardonius' son Artontes (mentioned in connection with rewards for burying Mardonius after the battle).
per-milon: A renowned Greek wrestler of Croton whose daughter Democedes became engaged to marry, to show Darius his influence and status.
per-arpoxais: One of three sons of Targitaïs; according to Scythian genealogy, father of the Katiari and Traspians clans.
per-colaxais: Youngest son of Targitaüs and founder of Scythian kingship, who received the sacred golden implements from the sky and established three lordships for his descendants, the greatest of which guarded the gold.
per-phoebus: Apollo, god of prophecy and healing, to whom Aristeas was possessed when he visited distant northern lands.
per-laodice: One of two Hyperborean maidens sent by the Hyperboreans to Delos bearing offerings, who never returned and was thereafter honored by the Delians.
per-agathyrsus: Son of Heracles and a serpent-woman, one of three brothers born to the woman; he and his brother Gelonus failed to meet their mother's test and left Scythia, while their younger brother Scythes succeeded and became ancestor of the Scythian kings.
per-hyperoche: A Hyperborean maiden sent by her people to Delos bearing offerings to Eileithyia, who never returned and was subsequently honored by the Delians.
per-strattis: Tyrant of Chios, whom Ionian conspirators sought to assassinate during the Persian Wars.
per-prometheus: A figure from Greek mythology, cited as the husband of Asia and namesake of the continent Asia, though his historicity is disputed.
per-scopasis: A Scythian king who ruled one of three divisions of the royal people and led the Sauromatae in the strategy against Darius' Persian invasion, tasked with defending the Tanaïs river and the Maeetian lake.
per-themison: A Theraean trader at Oaxus who, tricked by Etearchus into swearing an oath, was ordered to drown the king's daughter Phronime but instead fulfilled the letter of his oath by lowering her into the sea and retrieving her, then bringing her safely to Thera.
per-polymnestus: Father of Battus, a notable Theraean who took the pregnant Phronime as his concubine and fathered the stammering boy later known as Battus, founder of Cyrene.
per-spargapithes: A Scythian king whose son Gnurus was the grandfather of Anacharsis; he was treacherously killed by Spargapithes, king of the Agathyrsi, and his son Ariapithes succeeded him as king of Scythia.
per-autesion: An ancestor of Theras and great-grandfather of Argeia (wife of Aristodemus), descended from Polynices through the line of Thersander and Tisamenus.
per-learchus: Brother of Arcesilaus of Cyrene who strangled him after his military defeat in Libya, only to be killed in turn by Arcesilaus' wife Eryxo.
per-demonax: A respected citizen of Mantinea sent by the Mantineans to Cyrene as a mediator, who reorganized the Cyrenean state into three tribes and redistributed royal prerogatives to the people.
per-gygaea: Sister of Alexander of Macedon and daughter of Amyntas; married to the Persian Bubares and mother of Amyntas of Asia.
per-lysagoras: Father of Histiaeus, tyrant of Miletus whom Darius held at Susa.
per-pigres: A Carian, son of Hysseldomus, who commanded ships in Xerxes' fleet during the invasion of Greece.
per-ibanollis: Father of Heraclides of Mylasa, a Carian leader who ambushed the Persians at Pedasus during the Ionian Revolt.
per-demarmenus: A Spartan, father of Prinetadas and grandfather of a wife of Cleomenes (6.65 specifies his daughter Percalus was betrothed to Leotychides before being married by Demaratus).
per-antichares: A man of Eleon who advised Dorieus to establish a colony at Heraclea in Sicily based on oracles of Laius.
per-polydorus: A legendary king of Thebes, grandfather of Laius and great-grandson of Cadmus, known from genealogical tradition.
per-euryleon: A Spartan colonist who alone survived the battle in Sicily where Dorieus' expedition was destroyed, subsequently took Minoa, helped overthrow the tyrant Pithagoras of Selinus, attempted to rule Selinus himself, but was killed at an altar by the people.
per-iamid: An Elean diviner of the Iamid clan who fled to Croton and aided them against Sybaris because he could obtain no favorable omens while sacrificing for Sybaris' king Telys.
per-thebe: Daughter of the river-god Asopus and sister of Aegina, invoked by the Thebans as an avenger against Aegina through an oracle.
per-scaeus: A boxer who dedicated a tripod to Apollo at Delphi, possibly the son of Hippocoon and contemporary with Oedipus.
per-cineas: King of the Thessalians from Conium, who led a thousand horsemen sent to aid the Pisistratidae against the Spartan Anchimolius at Phalerum.
per-alcmaeonidae: An aristocratic Athenian clan held responsible for the death of the tyrant-aspirant Cylon and his followers and later accused of signaling to the Persians during the Persian Wars.
per-philocyprus: King of Soli in Cyprus, father of Aristocyprus; praised by Solon of Athens for his rule.
per-siromus: Grandfather of Onesilus, king of Salamis in Cyprus, and father of Chersis; ancestor of the Cypriot royal line in the early fifth century BC.
per-asopus: A river-god whose daughters were Thebe, Aegina, and Oeroe; his river flows from Cithaeron into the Plataeaean plain.
per-olorus: King of Thrace whose daughter Hegesipyle married Miltiades, ruler of the Chersonese.
per-phrynichus: An Athenian tragic playwright who composed "The Fall of Miletus," a drama about the Persian destruction of Miletus that so moved the audience that the city fined him and banned future performances of the work.
per-metiochus: Eldest son of Miltiades by a second wife; captured by Phoenicians while commanding a ship fleeing the Chersonese, brought before Darius, who rewarded him with a house, lands, and a Persian wife.
per-percalus: Daughter of Demarmenus, betrothed to Leotychides but married instead by Demaratus, causing Leotychides to turn against him.
per-agis: Ancestor of Leonidas, king of Sparta, in the line of descent from Heracles through Eurysthenes.
per-astrabacus: A hero with a shrine at Sparta whose precinct stood at the courtyard doors and who, according to local seers, fathered the Spartan king Demaratus.
per-periallus: Pythia (priestess of Apollo at Delphi) who was bribed by Cleomenes to pronounce that Demaratus was not the son of Ariston, and was later deposed for this corruption.
per-diactorides: A Scopad from Crannon in Thessaly, suitor of Agariste of Athens at the contest held by Cleisthenes.
per-leoprepes: Father of Theasides, a man of repute at Sparta who dissuaded the Aeginetans from carrying away King Leutychides; also father of the poet Simonides of Ceos.
per-epicydes: Father of Glaucus, a Lacedaemonian of three generations before Leutychides' time, renowned for justice.
per-epizelus: An Athenian soldier at Marathon who was suddenly struck blind during the battle, though suffering no physical wound, and attributed his loss of sight to encountering a supernatural apparition.
per-aeschines: A prominent Eretrian who revealed to the Athenians that the city was divided between those planning flight and traitors, and advised the Athenian defenders to withdraw before the Persian attack on Eretria.
per-pericles: Son of Xanthippus and Agariste, born from a prophetic lion-dream, who would become a leading Athenian statesman.
per-aristogeiton: Athenian tyrannicide who, along with Harmodius, killed Hipparchus son of Pisistratus but failed to end the tyranny, and whose fame for liberating Athens Herodotus considers less deserved than that of the Alcmeonidae.
per-phidon: Tyrant of Argos who standardized weights and measures for the Peloponnesians, held the Olympic contests himself by driving out the Elean organizers, and acted with exceptional arrogance toward other Greeks.
per-onomacritus: An Athenian diviner who organized the oracles of Musaeus, banished by Hipparchus for forging prophecies, and later persuaded Xerxes to invade Greece by selectively reciting favorable oracles.
per-artaeus: A Persian, father of Azanes (commander of Sogdians in Xerxes' army) and of Artachaees (overseer of the canal-digging at Athos).
per-hipponicus: Athenian of the wealthy Alcmeonid family; father of Callias; distinguished for his hatred of tyranny.
per-ariaramnes: An ancestor of Darius in the Achaemenid royal line, and also a Persian friend of the Ionians whose presence at Salamis contributed to Xerxes' execution of slanderous Phoenicians.
per-andromeda: Daughter of Cepheus and wife of Perseus, mother of Perses, ancestor of the Persians according to Greek mythological genealogy cited by Herodotus.
per-gergis: A Persian general in Xerxes' invasion force, son of Ariazus, commanding one division of the army as it marched inland from Doriscus toward Acanthus.
per-ithamitres: Nephew of Artayntes son of Artachaees, chosen to share command of the Persian fleet wintering at Samos after the battle of Salamis.
per-smerdomenes: Son of Otanes and cousin of Xerxes, serving as one of the generals commanding a third of the Persian infantry during the invasion of Greece.
per-teaspis: Father of Pharandates, a Persian commander of the Mares and Colchians in Xerxes' invasion force.
per-ariomardus: Brother of Artyphius and leader of the Caspians in Xerxes' invasion army.
per-pharandates: A Persian officer, son of Teaspis, who commanded the Mares and Colchians in Xerxes' army and was present at the Battle of Plataea.
per-persephone:
UNKNOWN

The passages mention "goddesses of the underworld" and "Eleusinian Demeter" in religious contexts, but Persephone is never named or clearly identified in these excerpts.
per-damasithymus: King of the Calyndians in Xerxes' fleet; rammed and killed by Artemisia at the Battle of Salamis.
per-aenesidemus: A Sicilian ruler of Acragas, father of Theron, who expelled Terillus from Himera.
per-theron: Tyrant of Acragas in Sicily who, having expelled Terillus from Himera, joined Gelon in defeating the Carthaginian Amilcas on the same day as the Greek victory at Salamis.
per-orithyia: Daughter of Erechtheus, ancient king of Athens, and wife of Boreas the north wind; invoked by the Athenians as their connection to Boreas when seeking divine aid against the Persian fleet.
per-aeolus: Father of Athamas, ancestor of the line involved in the human sacrifice ritual at Alus in Achaea that Xerxes learned of and respected during his invasion of Greece.
per-cytissorus: Son of Phrixus, whose descendants in Achaea were subject to ritual sacrifice as divine punishment for rescuing Athamas from the altar.
per-thetis: A sea-goddess (Nereid) to whom Persian Magi made sacrificial offerings at Sepia to calm a storm during Xerxes' invasion of Greece, identified by local Ionic tradition as the consort of Peleus.
per-eurymachus: Father of Leontiades, the Theban general at Thermopylae whose son Eurymachus was later killed by the Plataeans.
per-ischenous: Father of Pytheas, an Aeginetan captured fighting heroically at Artemisium.
per-micythus: A servant (likely regent) of Anaxilaus left in charge of Rhegium, who was later banished and settled in Tegea, having previously sent three thousand Rhegians to aid the Tarentines in a disastrous conflict.
per-pylagori: The Pylagori were magistrates or officials of the Amphictyonic council who, acting at Pylae, placed a price on the head of Epialtes for betraying the Greeks at Thermopylae.
per-hegesilaus: An ancestor of the Spartan king Leonidas and a progenitor in the genealogy of the second Spartan royal house.
per-athenades: A Trachinian who killed Epialtes, the traitor who revealed the mountain path at Thermopylae, for reasons Herodotus promises to explain later.
per-corydallus: A man from Anticyra mentioned in an alternative account of the mountain path at Thermopylae, but Herodotus discounts his involvement in favor of Epialtes the Trachinian.
per-abronichus: An Athenian courier, son of Lysicles, stationed with Leonidas at Thermopylae to relay news of the land army to the Greeks at Artemisium.
per-eurytus: A Spartan hoplite among the three hundred at Thermopylae who, suffering from ophthalmia and dismissed from camp, chose to return to battle and was killed when he learned of the Persian flanking movement.
per-dieneces: A Spartan hoplite distinguished for his courage at Thermopylae, famous for his defiant quip that if the Persian arrows hid the sun, the Greeks could fight in the shade.
per-cercopes: A legendary band of mischievous creatures whose seats along the Anopaea path near Alpenus marked its narrowest point.
per-euryclides: Father of Eurybiades, the Spartan admiral who commanded the Greek fleet at Artemisium and Salamis.
per-ocytus: Father of the Corinthian admiral Adimantus, who commanded Corinthian forces at Artemisium and Salamis during the Persian Wars.
per-mnesiphilus: An Athenian who advised Themistocles to persuade Eurybiades to keep the Greek fleet at Salamis rather than withdraw to the Isthmus.
per-scyllias: A diver from Scione who salvaged Persian property after the shipwreck at Pelion and deserted to the Greeks at Artemisium, where he informed the admirals of the Persian fleet's losses and the ships sent around Euboea.
per-autonous: A native hero of Delphi whose precinct lay near the Castalian spring below the Hyarapean Peak, credited with defending the sanctuary during the Persian invasion.
per-iacchus: A mystical cry heard during the Eleusinian festival, invoked by initiates as a divine voice that Dicaeus interprets as an omen protecting Athens and her allies against Xerxes' army.
per-theocydes: Athenian, father of Dicaeus, the exile who reported witnessing a supernatural portent near Eleusis with Demaratus during Xerxes' invasion.
per-ameinias: An Athenian from Pallene who initiated the naval engagement at Salamis by charging and ramming a Persian ship when other Greeks were retreating.
per-androdamas: Father of Theomestor, a Samian whom the Persians appointed tyrant of Samos after the naval battle at Salamis.
per-temenus: Temenus was an Argive ancestor whose three sons—Gauanes, Aeropus, and Perdiccas—fled Argos and founded the Macedonian royal dynasty.
per-alcetes: A Macedonian of the royal line, grandfather of Amyntas and great-grandfather of Alexander.
per-hyacinthus: A Spartan hero-god whose festival delayed the Spartans' response to the Athenian request for aid against the Persians.
per-thorax: A Thessalian from Larissa, son of Aleuas, who facilitated Mardonius' passage into Greece after having previously aided Xerxes' retreat from Athens.
per-gauanes: One of three exiled brothers of the Argive Temenid line who came to Macedonia via Illyria and worked as royal herdsmen, his youngest brother Perdiccas founding the Macedonian dynasty.
per-larissa: Thorax of Larissa, a Thessalian ruler who facilitated Xerxes' retreat and later opened passage for Mardonius into Greece during the Persian invasion.
per-harmocydes: A Phocian general who led a thousand hoplites to join Mardonius in Boeotia and exhorted his men to fight rather than be slaughtered by Persian cavalry.
per-theseus: A legendary Athenian hero whose pride in hiding Helen from the Tyndaridae prompted the Deceleans to betray him to them at Aphidnae.
per-hegetorides: A Coan, father of a woman who was the concubine of the Persian Pharandates and sought refuge with Pausanias after the battle of Plataea.
per-iamidae: Iamidae is a priestly clan of Elis to which Tisamenus, the diviner who sacrificed for the Greeks at Plataea, belonged.
per-artaynte: Daughter of Masistes and his wife, wife of Xerxes' son Darius, with whom Xerxes fell in love and took as his own concubine, ultimately provoking his wife Amestris to terrible vengeance.
per-xenagoras: A Greek from Halicarnassus who intervened to prevent Artayntes from killing Masistes, son of Darius, after the Persian defeat at Mykale, and was rewarded by Xerxes with the rulership of Cilicia.
per-timagenidas: A Theban leader who sided with the Persians and, facing Greek siege after Plataea, persuaded the Thebans to surrender him and Attaginus to Pausanias rather than endure prolonged devastation.
per-inachus: A legendary king of Argos, father of Io, whom the Phoenicians abducted in the opening narrative of Herodotus' inquiry into the origins of conflict between Greeks and barbarians.
per-philocyon: A Spartan warrior of the "irens" (elite unit) who fell at Plataea and was honored with burial in the Lacedaemonian tomb.
per-iardanus: A figure from Lydian genealogy, owner of a female slave by whom Heracles fathered the Heraclidae who subsequently ruled Sardis.
per-hermolycus: An Athenian pancratium athlete and son of Euthoenus who fought with greatest distinction at Plataea, later killed in combat against the Carystians near Geraestus.
per-myrsilus: Candaules, last Heraclid king of Sardis, whom the Greeks called Myrsilus; his rule preceded the rise of the Mermnadae dynasty under Croesus.
per-ninus: Legendary ancestor of the Heraclid dynasty that ruled Sardis, father of Agron who became the first Heraclid king.
per-dascylus: Father of Gyges, a bodyguard of the Lydian king Candaules.
per-archilochus: A poet of Paros who composed iambic verses mentioning Gyges, living roughly contemporary with that Lydian king.
per-zeus-of-the-hearth: One of the three epithets by which Croesus invokes Zeus in his grief after his son's accidental death at the hands of a guest-friend he had purified.
per-pittacus: One of two sages (the other being Bias of Priene) credited with dissuading Croesus from building a fleet to attack the Greek islands by warning him of the islanders' counter-strategy.
per-zeus-the-purifier: An epithet of Zeus invoked by Croesus at the death of his son Atys, killed by his guest Adrastus, whom Croesus himself had purified of blood-guilt.
per-dorus: Son of Hellen and eponymous ancestor of the Dorian Greeks, who inhabited Histiaean lands in the region below Ossa and Olympus.
per-aristolaides: Aristolaides, father of Lycurgus, an Athenian leader of the plain faction in early sixth-century Athens.
per-hellen: Eponymous ancestor of the Hellenes (Greeks); father of Dorus, whose people inhabited the land of Phthia in ancient times before their subsequent migrations.
per-phya: A tall woman from the Paeanian deme dressed as Athena by Megacles and Pisistratus to deceive the Athenians into welcoming Pisistratus back to power.
per-pallenian-athena: A temple in Attica near Marathon where Pisistratus' returning army encountered Athenian forces marching out to oppose him.
per-alcmeonid: An Athenian family said to be under a curse, whose member Megacles allied with Pisistratus and later broke with him over a marital slight.
per-alcmeonids: An Athenian aristocratic clan whose members were exiled from Athens during Pisistratus' third tyranny.
per-zeus-of-comrades: A epithet of Zeus invoked by Croesus after his guest Adrastus accidentally killed his son, representing Zeus as guardian of the bond between guest-friends (xenia).
per-hegesicles: One of two Spartan kings during whose joint reign the Lacedaemonians achieved military success except against the Tegeans, before Lycurgus reformed their constitution.
per-aryenis: A Lydian princess, daughter of Alyattes, given in marriage to Astyages of the Medes to seal a peace treaty between Lydia and Media.
per-chromios: One of three Argive survivors in the three-hundred-man battle against Sparta over Thyrea, who fled after the battle.
per-dindymene: A mountain in Asia Minor sacred to the Mother Goddess, from which the Hermus River originates.
per-leobetes: A Spartan king, nephew of Lycurgus, during whose guardianship Lycurgus introduced the constitutional reforms that transformed Sparta's governance.
per-madyes: King of the Scythians who led an invasion of Asia and defeated Cyaxares' Median forces while they were besieging Ninus.
per-athena-proneia: Athena Proneia (or Pronaia) is an epithet form of Athena worshipped at Delphi, to whose temple Croesus dedicated a golden shield.
per-alcenor: An Argive soldier, one of three survivors of the three-hundred-man battle against Lacedaemon over Thyrea, who fled to Argos claiming victory but was contradicted by the Lacedaemonian Othryades' stance at the battlefield.
per-protothyes: King of the Scythians, father of Madyes, who led Scythian invasions into Asia during the reign of Cyaxares.
per-tyrrhenus: Son of King Atys of Lydia, he led a band of Lydians fleeing famine across the sea and eventually to Italy, where they became known as Tyrrhenians after his name.
per-proneia: A goddess with a temple at Delphi where Croesus dedicated a golden shield.
per-achaemenidae: The royal clan of Persia, belonging to the Pasargadae tribe and providing the kings of Persia.
per-spako: A Median slave woman, wife of the cowherd Mitradates, whom Astyages ordered to expose the infant Cyrus in the mountains (her name, meaning "dog" in Median, was Cyno in Greek).
per-agasicles: A man of Halicarnassus who violated the Triopian Apollo temple law by taking home a bronze tripod won at the games, causing the five other Dorian cities to ban Halicarnassus from the temple.
per-pythennos: A Phocaean envoy sent by the Ionians and Aeolians to Sparta to plead for military aid against Persian expansion, but rejected by the Lacedaemonians.
per-heavenly-one: Not a person but a deity—Aphrodite, worshipped at an ancient temple in Ascalon in Syria that Scythian raiders plundered, incurring her curse of infertility upon them and their descendants.
per-triopian-apollo: A god worshipped at a shared temple in the Dorian cities of the southwestern coast of Asia Minor, where victors in games dedicated bronze tripods as offerings.
per-lacrines: A Spartan envoy sent to Cyrus at Sardis to deliver the Lacedaemonians' warning that he must not harm Greek cities.
per-carian-zeus: A deity worshipped at Mylasa in Caria, venerated by Carians, Mysians, and Lydians as connected to their common ancestry.
per-kings-eye: A role assigned in a children's game played by the young Cyrus, serving as an official to monitor and report on the other child-players.
per-hippolochus: A legendary ancestor of Lycian kings, referenced in determining Ionian lineage and kingship claims.
per-mitra: The Persian name for Aphrodite, the goddess of love worshipped by the Persians after learning the practice from Assyrians and Arabians.
per-mysus: A legendary figure the Carians claimed as brother of Lydus and Car, and ancestor of the Mysians.
per-cityguarding-athena: A sanctuary in Chios where Pactyes took refuge before being surrendered to the Persians.
per-car: Car was, according to Carian tradition, the eponymous ancestor of the Carians, brother to Lydus and Mysus, and worshipped at an ancient shrine of Carian Zeus at Mylasa.
per-bel: A Babylonian god (identified by Herodotus with Zeus) worshipped in Babylon, whose sacred enclosure contains a great tower with a shrine at its summit where a priestess chosen by the god spends the night.
per-zeus-belus: A deity of Babylon with a sacred enclosure in the city's center, housing an eight-towered shrine where a priestess chosen by the god kept vigil nightly.
per-hystapes: An Achaemenid nobleman, father of the young Darius, whom Cyrus suspects of plotting against him after dreaming of Darius with wings overshadowing Asia and Europe.
per-olympian-zeus: A temple at Pisa used as a geographical reference point for measuring distance in Egypt.
per-amun: A supreme Egyptian deity, identified by Herodotus with Zeus, whom the inhabitants of Meroe in Ethiopia worship and consult through an oracle that directs their military campaigns.
per-theban-zeus: A deity worshipped at Thebes in Egypt, said by Egyptians to visit his shrine at night where a woman sleeps in the temple and refrains from intercourse with men.
per-great-king: The title for the Persian king; Herodotus notes he drank only boiled water from the Choaspes river, carried in silver vessels on mule-drawn wagons during campaigns.
per-amytheon: Father of Melampus, the legendary Greek prophet who introduced Dionysian worship to Greece from Egypt.
per-amon: The Egyptian name for Zeus, worshipped especially at Thebes where rams are considered sacred and not sacrificed except once yearly at Zeus' festival.
per-pan: A god worshipped by the Mendesians of Egypt, identified with a sacred he-goat and represented in Egyptian and Greek art with goat's head and legs.
per-themis: A Greek goddess whose name Herodotus believes did not originate in Egypt, unlike most other Greek divine names.
per-thasian-heracles: A cult title of Heracles worshipped at Thasos, whose temple there was founded by Phoenician settlers five generations before the birth of Heracles son of Amphitryon.
per-timarete: One of the three priestesses at the oracle of Dodona, second in seniority after Promeneia.
per-promeneia: One of the three eldest priestesses at the oracle of Dodona, custodian of its traditional account of the sanctuary's divine foundation.
per-nicandra: A priestess at the oracle of Dodona, the youngest of three priestesses and a transmitter of the temple's traditional account of the oracle's foundation.
per-lynceus: An ancestor of Perseus according to Egyptian tradition, one of two men (along with Danaus) said by the people of Khemmis to have traveled from their city to Greece.
per-gorgon: A monster slain by Perseus, who brought her head from Libya as part of his travels to Egypt.
per-rameses-ii: An Egyptian king of the second dynasty, renowned for extensive military campaigns across the Red Sea region and mainland Asia, marked by erected pillars commemorating his conquests.
per-phthius: An Achaean, father of Arkhandrus and father-in-law of Danaus, whose descendant's name was borne by an Egyptian town.
per-anhur: Anhur is an Egyptian god (identified with Ares by the Greeks) worshipped at Papremis, where an annual festival involves a violent ritual reenactment commemorating his forcible entry to his mother's temple.
per-diomedes: A Greek hero whose prowess is recounted in Homer's Iliad, mentioned here in connection with the story of Helen and Alexander's voyage to Sidon.
per-hades: The underworld of the Greeks, into which the Egyptian king Rhampsinitus descended alive to play dice with Demeter and receive a golden gift.
per-pharaoh: Pheros, pharaoh of Egypt who succeeded Sesostris, was struck blind after hurling a spear into the flooding Nile, regained his sight via the urine of a faithful wife, whom he married while burning the other women he had tested.
per-polydamna: Wife of Thon, an Egyptian, from whom Helene obtained magical drugs according to Homer's *Odyssey*.
per-thon: An Egyptian whose wife Polydamna possessed magical drugs, mentioned in Homer's Odyssey as a figure of knowledge in Egyptian tradition.
per-philitis: A shepherd who pastured flocks near the pyramids during a period of Egyptian misery, after whom the pyramids were popularly named.
per-cheops: An Egyptian pharaoh who built a pyramid at Giza with massive labor expenditures on materials and provisions for the workforce.
per-hephaestopolis: Father of Iadmon the Samian, owner of the courtesan Rhodopis and the fabulist Aesop.
per-king-rhampsinitus: An Egyptian king whose reign was prosperous and well-governed, after whom Kheops brought misery to Egypt through forced labor and temple closures.
per-chephren: Chephren was a pharaoh of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty who built one of the great pyramids at Giza, the construction of which Herodotus describes in detail regarding its methods and costs.
per-xanthes: A man of Samos who brought the courtesan Rhodopis to Egypt, where she was later freed by Kharaxus of Mytilene.
per-anysis: A blind Egyptian king whose reign was interrupted when the Ethiopian Sabacos invaded Egypt; Anysis fled to the marshes while Sabacos ruled for fifty years.
per-archidice: A courtesan of Naucratis whose fame spread throughout Greece, celebrated in song though less renowned than Rhodopis.
per-scamandronymus: Father of Kharaxus of Mytilene and of the poetess Sappho.
per-sabacon: An Ethiopian king who invaded and ruled Egypt for fifty years, during which he imposed constructive rather than capital punishment on wrongdoers by requiring them to build embankments.
per-sennacherib: King of Assyria who invaded Egypt with Arab allies during the reign of the Egyptian priest-king Sethos, but whose army was allegedly destroyed by divine intervention at Pelusium.
per-sanacharib: King of Assyria who invaded Egypt with a great force of Arabians and Assyrians, but was defeated at Pelusium when field mice destroyed his army's weapons during the night.
per-bubastis: Artemis, identified with the Egyptian goddess worshipped at her temple, according to Egyptian theology equated with Demeter as Isis.
per-sardanapallus: A legendary king of the Assyrian city of Ninus, said to have accumulated great wealth in an underground treasury that thieves attempted to steal by tunneling.
per-thannyras: Son of Inaros, an Egyptian who received sovereignty from the Persians despite his father's rebellion against them.
per-sethos: A priest of Hephaestus who became king of Egypt, rejected the warrior class, and faced the Assyrian king Sanacharib's invasion with only merchants and craftsmen, whom he led to miraculous victory at Pelusium through divine intervention.
per-typho: Typho is a mythological figure whom local tradition claimed was hidden beneath the Serbonian marsh on the border between Syria and Egypt.
per-egyptus: Mythical king whose sons pursued the fleeing daughters of Danaus, who then founded Athena's temple at Lindos, per Herodotus.
per-set: An Egyptian god whom the Greeks identified with Typhon, and whom Horus deposed as the last divine ruler of Egypt before human priests took power.
per-lord-cambyses: Persian king (r. 530–522 BC) who conquered Egypt, took Memphis, and tested the deposed Egyptian king Psammenitus' resolve through displays of cruelty before showing clemency.
per-pausiris: Son of Amyrtaeus, an Egyptian to whom the Persians restored his father's sovereign power over Egypt, exemplifying Persian custom toward rebellious kings' sons.
per-hophra: Egyptian pharaoh who ruled for twenty-five years after his father Psammis, sent an army against Cyrene where it suffered great defeat, and was subsequently overthrown by rebellious Egyptians who believed he had deliberately sacrificed them to secure his power.
per-persian-king: Cambyses, king of Persia, sent emissaries with gifts to the Ethiopian king seeking alliance, but was rebuffed with a message questioning his justice and military capability.
per-telecles: Father of Theodorus, a renowned gem-engraver of Samos whose seal-ring Polycrates cast into the sea as a sacrifice.
per-pataici: A dwarf-shaped divine image that the Phoenicians carried on the prows of their triremes and revered in their temples.
per-pantagnotus: Brother of Polycrates of Samos; initially granted a share of power in Samos but later put to death by Polycrates as the latter consolidated sole rule.
per-lycopas: A Lacedaemonian who died fighting bravely at Samos when he and Archias entered the fortress during the Samian conflict.
per-dictyna: A goddess worshipped at Cydonia in Crete, for whom the Samians built a shrine during their five-year settlement there.
per-naustrophus: Father of Eupalinus, the Megarian engineer who designed the famous tunnel through the mountain at Samos.
per-eupalinus: A Megarian engineer who designed the famous tunnel through the mountain at Samos, carrying water from a spring to the city.
per-amphicrates: A king of Samos whose reign preceded the Samians' expedition to Crete, under whom Samians raided Aegina and suffered mutual losses, causing subsequent Aeginetan enmity.
per-philes: A Samian, father of Rhoecus who built the great temple at Samos.
per-achaemenids: The royal house of Persia, descendants of Achaemenes, to whom Cambyses appeals to recover the throne from Median usurpers.
per-cranaspes: Son of Mitrobates, governor of Dascyleium; killed by the satrap Oroetes during the Magi's rule in Persia.
per-calliphon: Father of Democedes, a physician of Croton renowned for his medical skill in the time of Polycrates.
per-rhoecus: A Samian architect who initiated construction of the great temple at Samos, one of the three greatest engineering works of the Greeks.
per-telesarchus: A man of consequence among the Samian citizens who spoke against Maeandrius' retention of tyrannical power.
per-caustrobius: Father of Aristeas of Proconnesus, a poet whose account of northern lands Herodotus references.
per-vidarna: A Persian of high rank who joined Otanes and the other conspirators against the Magus usurper Smerdis.
per-perpherees: Five Hyperborean men sent as escorts with maidens bearing offerings to Delos, now honored there as heroes of the tradition.
per-from-scythes: Legendary ancestor of the Scythian kings, son of Heracles and a serpent-woman, who alone among his brothers fulfilled the tests his mother set and thus became founder of the royal line.
per-eileithyia: A goddess of childbirth, to whom Hyperborean maidens Hyperoche and Laodice brought tribute in gratitude for easing labor.
per-sciton: A servant attending Democedes who accumulated considerable gold by collecting staters dropped by Darius' wives as they rewarded Democedes for healing the king.
per-abaris: A legendary Hyperborean reputed to have traveled the world while fasting, carried by a magical arrow, whom Herodotus declines to elaborate upon.
per-asies: Son of Cotys and grandson of Manes, claimed by the Lydians as the namesake of Asia (rather than Prometheus' wife), from whom the Asiad clan at Sardis derived its name.
per-cotys: A Lydian ancestral figure, father of Asies, from whom the Asiads clan at Sardis claimed descent.
per-goetosyrus: The Scythian name for Apollo, according to their religious practices and pantheon.
per-apia: The Scythian name for Earth, whom Herodotus identifies as the wife of Zeus in Scythian religion.
per-hippolaus: A promontory on the northern coast of the Black Sea between the Borysthenes and Hypanis rivers, named for a figure otherwise unidentified in the surviving record.
per-teaspes: Father of Sataspes, an Achaemenid whose son was sent by King Xerxes to sail around Libya as punishment for rape, but failed to complete the voyage.
per-firegiver: A figure in Lydian mythology, alternative name for Prometheus, whose wife Asia is said by most Greeks to have given her name to the continent of Asia.
per-papaeus: Papaeus is the Scythian name for Zeus.
per-tabiti: Hestia in Scythian religious practice, foremost among the deities worshipped by the Scythians in general.
per-argimpasa: The Scythian name for Aphrodite Ourania (Heavenly Aphrodite), whom the Scythians worshipped among their principal deities.
per-bacchic-dionysus: God of wine and ecstasy worshipped in Greek mystery religions, whose initiation rites the Scythian king Scyles undergoes in the Greek city of Borysthenes, causing scandal among his people.
per-gebeleizis: A deity of the Thracians, alternative name for Salmoxis, to whom they believe the dead go and to whom they send human messengers by throwing them onto spear-points.
per-thagimasadas: Scythian name for Poseidon, worshipped especially by the Royal Scythians.
per-gnurus: Son of Lycus and father of Anacharsis, a member of the Scythian royal family.
per-opoea: A Scythian woman, wife of King Scyles and mother of his son Oricus, whom Scyles inherited along with his father's kingdom after Ariapithes' death.
per-oricus: Son of Scyles and the Scythian woman Opoea, born to the Scythian king who adopted Greek ways.
per-mnesarchus: Father of Pythagoras, the philosopher of Samos.
per-ariantas: A Scythian king who commissioned a bronze vessel made from collected arrowheads as a census memorial in the region of Exampaeus between the Borysthenes and Hypanis rivers.
per-erxander: Father of Cöes, general of the Mytilenaeans, mentioned in Darius' Scythian campaign.
per-teres: King of Thrace and father of Octamasades' mother, whose brother Sitalces negotiates with Octamasades to recover him in exchange for the fugitive Scyles.
per-iphigenia: A daughter of Agamemnon whom the Tauri of the Crimea worship as their Virgin goddess and identify with the priestess to whom they sacrifice shipwrecked men and captured Greeks.
per-metrodorus: A tyrant of Proconnesus in the Hellespont who supported Darius' plan against the advice of Miltiades.
per-herophantus: A ruler of Parium in the Hellespont who favored Darius and opposed Miltiades' plan.
per-hippoclus: Ruler of Lampsacus on the Hellespont, one of the prominent men who voted in favor of Darius' plan against Miltiades' proposal.
per-aiaces: A tyrant of Samos favored by Darius who voted with the majority to keep the Hellespont bridge intact, not with Miltiades' proposal to destroy it.
per-taxakis: A Scythian king who commanded one of the three royal divisions against Darius' Persian invasion, uniting with Idanthyrsus' forces to harass the enemy while retreating eastward.
per-poeciles: Father of Membliarus, a Phoenician who settled descendants on the island later called Thera.
per-daphnis: Daphnis of Abydos, a ruler in Xerxes' court who voted in favor of Darius' plan against the advice of Miltiades.
per-aesanius: Father of Grinnus, king of Thera; ancestor in the line of descent from Theras.
per-eryxo: A Cyrenean woman, wife of Arcesilaus, who killed her husband's murderer Learchus.
per-lord-phoebus-apollo: The god of prophecy at Delphi who, through his priestess, commanded Battus to found a colony in Libya.
per-adicran: A Libyan king whose lands were seized by Greek colonists at Cyrene, and who appealed to the Egyptian king Apries for aid against them.
per-oeolycus: A Spartan who received the nickname "Oeolycus" (meaning "wolf-child") after refusing to sail with his father Theras, and whose son Aegeus gave his name to the Aegidae clan.
per-sostratus: A merchant of Aegina, son of Laodamas, who profited more than any other Greek from trade with Tartessus.
per-euphemus: A Minyan whose descendant Battus was chosen by the king of Thera to lead a colonial expedition to Libya, though Battus initially proved reluctant to undertake the mission.
per-colaeus: Captain of a Samian merchant ship blown off course to Platea and then to Tartessus, where he and his crew made an exceptionally profitable trade that led to lasting ties between Samos and the colonies of Cyrene and Thera.
per-arcesilauses: King of Cyrene who consulted the Delphic oracle about his return to power and received a prophecy warning him against baking amphoras in an oven and entering a tidal place.
per-battuses: Battuses are the alternating royal names in the dynasty ruling Cyrene, with four Battuses and four Arcesilauses prophesied by the Delphic oracle to hold kingship for eight generations before its end.
per-aglomachus: A Cyrenean private citizen who owned a tower where some of Cyrenaeans fled during Arcesilaus' reign of terror, only to be burned to death there by Arcesilaus.
per-hellenodicae: Officials appointed by the Olympic Games to judge contestants' eligibility and oversee competition, who determined that Alexander of Macedon was Greek and eligible to compete in the footrace.
per-lycaean-zeus: A hill near Cyrene in Libya, named for a local Zeus sanctuary, where Persian forces under Amasis camped after passing through the city.
per-molpagoras: Father of Aristagoras, who served as deputy ruler of Miletus.
per-iatragoras: An agent sent by Aristagoras to arrest Ionian tyrants who had opposed the expedition against Naxos.
per-sisamenes: A Persian royal judge, father of Otanes, whom Cambyses executed and flayed for accepting a bribe, then used his skin to cover the judicial seat.
per-erxandrus: Father of Coes, whom Darius appointed to rule Mytilene.
per-thessalus: A Spartan colonist who accompanied Dorieus to Sicily and was killed in battle against the Phoenicians and Egestans.
per-oliatus: A tyrant of Mylasa, son of Ibanollis, seized by Iatragoras on Aristagoras' orders during the Ionian Revolt.
per-mantyes: A Paeonian, brother of Pigres, who sought to rule his countrymen and demonstrated Paeonian customs to Darius at Sardis by sending his sister to perform multiple tasks simultaneously.
per-celees: A Spartan colonist who sailed with Dorieus to Sicily and was slain in battle against the Phoenicians and Egestans.
per-paraebates: A Spartan companion of Dorieus who sailed to Sicily to found a colony but was killed in battle against the Phoenicians and Egestans.
per-prinetadas: Father of the woman who became the second wife of a Spartan king Anaxandridas and bore him Cleomenes I.
per-aristogiton: An Athenian of Gephyraean descent who, along with Harmodius, slew Hipparchus son of Pisistratus, though the tyranny that followed proved even harsher.
per-labdacus: A legendary king of Thebes, father of Laius, in whose era (approximately) certain Cadmean inscriptions were believed to have been made.
per-butacides: Father of Philippus of Croton, a Greek whose son followed Dorieus to Libya and was slain there.
per-achaean-demeter: A goddess worshipped by the Gephyraeans at Athens with rites and mysteries not observed by other Athenians.
per-pithagoras: Tyrant of Selinus whom Euryleon deposed before being himself slain by the Selinuntians.
per-teleboae: A people whose spoils Amphitryon dedicated at the temple of Ismenian Apollo in Thebes, according to an inscription on a tripod.
per-neleus: Neleus was a legendary ancestor of the Pisistratid dynasty, founder of the house of Pylos from which the Pisistratae claimed descent.
per-hippocoon: Father of Scaeus, a boxer, whose son dedicated a tripod at Apollo's shrine; placed by Herodotus in the age of Oedipus.
per-alcmaeonid: An Athenian clan to which Cleisthenes belonged, prominent in Athenian politics and said to have bribed the Pythian priestess to support their interests.
per-aegicores: One of the four ancient Ionic tribes of Attica, replaced by Cleisthenes' ten new tribal divisions in his democratic reforms at Athens.
per-argades: One of the four Ionic tribal divisions named after the sons of Ion, superseded by Cleisthenes' ten new tribes.
per-nestor: A legendary king of Pylos, father of Pisistratus, whose name Hippocrates invoked by naming his son Pisistratus.
per-aster: A Spartan general, son of Aster, sent by the Lacedaemonians to drive out the Pisistratidae from Athens but killed by Thessalian cavalry at Phalerum.
per-geleon: One of the four original Ionian tribes of Athens, after whom Cleisthenes deliberately refused to name any of his newly created ten tribes.
per-ion: A legendary hero from whom four traditional Athenian tribes took their names (Geleon, Aegicores, Argades, and Hoples), whom Cleisthenes deliberately excluded when reorganizing Athens into ten new tribes.
per-hoples: One of the four Ionic tribal divisions that Cleisthenes replaced when reorganizing Athenian tribes into ten new groups.
per-aias: An Ajax, hero of Salamis, included by Cleisthenes among the ten Athenian tribal eponyms despite being non-Athenian, as a neighbor and ally of Athens.
per-talaus: Father of Adrastus, the Argive hero whose shrine stood in the marketplace of Sicyon.
per-astacus: Father of Melanippus, a Theban hero whom Cleisthenes of Sicyon imported to rival the cult of Adrastus.
per-polybus: A legendary king of Sicyon, maternal grandfather of Adrastus, who died without heir and bequeathed his kingship to Adrastus.
per-boeotian-thebes: A Boeotian city from which the tyrant Cleisthenes of Sicyon obtained the hero Melanippus to rival the cult of Adrastus in his own land.
per-tydeus: Son-in-law of Adrastus, whom Adrastus slew, making him Melanippus's deadliest enemy.
per-aegialeus: Son of Adrastus, eponymous ancestor of the Aegialeis tribe of Sicyon, which was named after him.
per-mecisteus: Brother of Tydeus, slain by Adrastus in the mythological conflict between Adrastus and the sons of Oedipus.
per-timesitheus: A Delphian of notable strength and courage, imprisoned under sentence of death by the Athenians after Cleomenes and Isagoras' seizure of the Acropolis failed.
per-echecrates: Father of Eetion, a man of the township of Petra and of Lapith lineage, whose son married Labda of the Bacchiadae and fathered the future tyrant Cypselus.
per-alcmaeonids: A prominent Athenian family who conspired with the Pythian priestess against the Pisistratidae tyrants and later benefited from Spartan intervention to restore democracy in Athens.
per-anthemus: A town in Macedonia offered by King Amyntas to the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias, who refused it.
per-aegina: An island state in the Saronic Gulf that the Thebans, guided by an oracle, appealed to for military aid against Theban enemies, with the Aeginetans responding by sending the Sons of Aeacus.
per-amphion: A member of the Corinthian oligarchy of the Bacchiadae, father of the crippled Labda who married Eetion and bore the future tyrant Cypselus.
per-iolcus: A Thessalian city offered to the exiled Athenian tyrant Hippias as a place of refuge, which he declined.
per-caeneus: A Lapith ancestor in whose lineage Eetion, husband of Labda, was reckoned.
per-cylon: An Olympian athlete who attempted to seize the Athenian acropolis but was killed by the naval presidents while taking sanctuary, an act attributed to the Alcmaeonidae and preceding Pisistratus' rise to power.
per-charopinus: Brother of Aristagoras and general of the Milesians appointed to lead the expedition against Sardis.
per-lapith: A man of the township of Petra, husband of Labda (daughter of Amphion), and ancestor of Eetion through the line of Caeneus.
per-hermophantus: A Milesian general appointed by Aristagoras to command forces in the campaign against Sardis during the Ionian Revolt.
per-melanthius: An Athenian citizen of unblemished reputation, appointed admiral of twenty ships sent to aid the Ionians against Persia.
per-euelthon: Grandfather of Gorgus and Onesilus, and earlier king of Salamis in Cyprus.
per-cybebe: A goddess worshipped in Lydia, whose temple at Sardis was burned by Ionians during their revolt, providing the Persians with justification for later temple destruction in Greece.
per-aristocyprus: King of the Solians who died fighting the Persians during the Cyprian revolt, son of Philocyprus whom Solon praised.
per-stesenor: Ruler of Curium in Cyprus who betrayed the Cyprian rebels during their revolt against Persia, causing their defeat.
per-eualcides: General of Eretria who fought with the Ionians at Ephesus, slain by the Persians for his renown as an athlete and poet-praised warrior.
per-white-pillars: A place in Caria near the river Marsyas where the Carians assembled to plan their defense against the Persian general Daurises during the Ionian Revolt.
per-hegesander: Father of Hecataeus the historian, mentioned only as a genealogical reference in a passage about the Ionian Revolt.
per-amorges: A Persian general under Darius I who was killed in an ambush set by Carians at Pedasus while leading an army against their cities.
per-sisimaces: A Persian general killed in an ambush at Pedasus when the Carians attacked the Persian force marching against their cities.
per-pythogenes: Brother of Scythes, king of Zancle, whom Hippocrates of Gela put in chains for losing the city to the Samians.
per-pixodarus: A Carian leader from Cindya, son of Mausolus and husband of the daughter of Syennesis of Cilicia, who proposed that the Carians face the Persians with the Maeander at their own backs to prevent retreat.
per-mylasas: Leader of Carian forces who ambushed and defeated a Persian army at Pedasus during the Ionian Revolt.
per-mausolus: Father of Pixodarus, a ruler of Caria whose descendant organized Carian resistance against Persian forces during the Ionian Revolt.
per-bisaltes: A man of Abydos, son of Apollophanes, left in charge of Hellespont affairs by Histiaeus the Milesian.
per-hegesipyle: Daughter of Olorus, king of Thrace, whom Miltiades married to consolidate his control of the Chersonese.
per-apollophanes: Father of Bisaltes of Abydos, who was left by Histiaeus to command the Hellespont.
per-philaeus: Philaeus son of Ajax, the first member of Miltiades' family to become an Athenian citizen, establishing the family's Athenian lineage.
per-alcidas: Alcidas was a Spartan whose son Agetus married the woman who had been transformed from ugliness to beauty and subsequently became the wife of King Ariston.
per-aristophantus: Father of Cobon, a man of influence at Delphi who was later implicated in the oracle's false judgment against Demaratus.
per-argeia: Wife of Aristodemus, daughter of Autesion, who bore Aristodemus twins and unwittingly revealed to the Lacedaemonians which child was the elder by her consistent care of him.
per-panites: A Messenian who advised the Lacedaemonians to observe the mother of Aristodemus' twins to determine which child was the elder.
per-artozostre: Daughter of Darius, given in marriage to Mardonius son of Gobryas, who led the Persian invasion force against Greece in 492 BC.
per-cyniscus: Son of Leutychides, king of Sparta, also called Zeuxidemus; died before his father and did not become king, leaving his son Archidemus as heir.
per-eurydame: Second wife of Spartan king Leutychides and mother of Lampito, who married her nephew Archidemus.
per-menius: Brother of Eurydame, the second wife of Spartan king Leutychides.
per-theasides: A man of repute at Sparta, son of Leoprepes, who dissuaded the Aeginetans from carrying off King Leutychides by warning them of Spartan retaliation.
per-cnoethus: Father of Nicodromus, an Aeginetan whose son conspired to betray the island to Athens.
per-casambus: A wealthy and prominent Aeginetan of noble lineage, son of Aristocrates, taken hostage to Athens by the Spartan kings Cleomenes and Leutychides.
per-lampito: A Spartan princess, daughter of King Leutychides, married to her nephew Archidemus, son of Zeuxidemus.
per-aristocrates: Father of Casambus, one of the ten most honored and powerful men of Aegina given as hostage to the Athenians by Cleomenes and Leutychides.
per-nothon: Father of Aeschines, a leading man of Eretria who advised the Athenians during the Persian attack on Euboea.
per-cleander: A prophet from Phigalea in Arcadia who persuaded the enslaved population of Tiryns to attack their masters, sparking a prolonged war with the Argive nobility.
per-euphorbus: Euphorbus son of Alcimachus, an Eretrian of repute who betrayed the city to the Persians during their siege in 490 BC.
per-deceles: An Athenian, father of Sophanes, who killed the Argive captain Eurybates in single combat during a war between Athens and Aegina.
per-alcimachus: Father of Euphorbus, an Eretrian whose son betrayed Eretria to the Persians during their invasion.
per-great-warrior: Artaxerxes I, son of Xerxes and Persian king (reigned c. 465-424 BC), whose name Herodotus glosses as "the Great Warrior" in Greek.
per-evagoras: Owner of mares that won three Olympic prizes in the four-horse chariot race, a Laconian.
per-couphagoras: Father of Epizelus, an Athenian who fought at Marathon.
per-stesilaus: An Athenian general who died fighting the Persians at Marathon.
per-philagrus: An Eretrian of repute, son of Cineas, who with Euphorbus son of Alcimachus betrayed Eretria to the Persians during Darius's invasion.
per-phaenippus: An Athenian, father of Callias, whose son was notably hostile to the tyrant Pisistratus.
per-thrasylaus: An Athenian, father of Stesilaus, who was one of the generals killed at the Battle of Marathon.
per-aristonymus: Father of Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon; grandfather of the tyrant's daughter Agariste.
per-smindyrides: A wealthy Greek from Sybaris in Italy, son of Hippocrates, known for his luxurious lifestyle, who came as a suitor to compete for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-myron: Grandfather of Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon, in the line of descent from which Cleisthenes' daughter Agariste would be married to a Greek suitor.
per-cynegirus: Athenian soldier who died at Marathon, his hand severed by an ax while seizing an enemy ship's figurehead.
per-epistrophus: Father of Amphimnestus, an Epidamnian suitor of Agariste of Sicyon.
per-amphimnestus: An Epidamnian suitor for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon, from the Ionian Gulf region.
per-amyris: Father of Damasus of Siris, called "the Wise," mentioned among suitors competing for the hand of Agariste of Sicyon.
per-titormus: An Aetolian renowned for surpassing all Greeks in strength, who withdrew from human society to the remote interior of Aetolia.
per-andreas: Ancestor of Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon, appearing in the genealogy as great-grandfather of Cleisthenes son of Aristonymus.
per-damasus: A suitor from Siris in Italy, son of Amyris the Wise, who competed for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-leocedes: Son of Phidon the tyrant of Argos, a suitor for the hand of Agariste daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-laphanes: An Azenian from Paeus, son of Euphorion (said to have hosted the Dioscuri), among the suitors competing for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-amiantus: An Arcadian from Trapezus, son of Lycurgus, who competed for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-lysanias: An Eretrian, the sole suitor from Euboea competing for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-hegesandrus: Father of Hecataeus, an early Greek historian who recorded an account of the Pelasgians' expulsion from Attica.
per-athens-megacles: An Athenian, son of Alcmaeon (who had visited Croesus), among suitors competing for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-onomastus: Son of Agaeus, from Elis, among the suitors competing for the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-alcon: Alcon, a Molossian, was a suitor seeking the hand of Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-agaeus: An Elean, father of Onomastus, one of the suitors who came to court Agariste, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon.
per-cypselids: A ruling family of Corinth to which the Athenian suitor Hippocleides was related by ancestry.
per-tisias: Father of Lysagoras, a man of Parian descent whose son slandered Miltiades to the Persian Hydarnes.
per-lasus: A scholar of Hermione who detected Onomacritus fabricating oracles in the writings of Musaeus, leading to the diviner's banishment by Hipparchus.
per-atreus: Legendary Greek king of Mycenae, father of Agamemnon and Menelaus, whose sons' expedition against Troy Herodotus cites as inferior in scale to Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
per-anaphes: A Cissian in Xerxes' army, son of Otanes, commanding the Cissians.
per-ormuzd: Charioteer of Xerxes, son of Otanes; this figure is actually named Patiramphes in the text, not Ormuzd.
per-patiramphes: A Persian charioteer, son of Otanes, who drove Xerxes' chariot during the king's passage across the Hellespont.
per-megapanus: Leader of the Hyrcanians in Xerxes' invasion force, later appointed governor of Babylon.
per-otaspes: Commander of the Assyrians and Chaldeans in Xerxes' invasion army, son of Artachaees.
per-thoas: A Pelasgian whose companions were killed by the women of Lemnos in an earlier massacre, subsequently invoked to characterize acts of exceptional cruelty.
per-pharnazathres: An Indian commander in Xerxes' invasion force, appointed to lead the Indian contingent.
per-artabates: A Persian, father of Pharnazathres, whose son commanded the Indian contingent in Xerxes' invasion army.
per-dadicae-artyphius: Commander of the Gandarians and Dadicae in Xerxes' invasion army of 480 BC.
per-sogdians-azanes: Commander of the Sogdians in Xerxes' army, son of Artaeus.
per-artyphius: Brother of Ariomardus, who led the Caspians in Xerxes' army.
per-pherendates: Commander of the Sarangae contingent in Xerxes' invasion army, son of Megabazus.
per-paricanians-siromitres: Commander of the Paricanians in Xerxes' invasion force.
per-arsamenes: Son of Darius, commander of the Utian and Mycian contingents in Xerxes' invasion army.
per-oarizus: A Libyan, father of Massages who commanded the Libyan contingent in Xerxes' invasion force.
per-dotus: Son of Megasidrus, commander of the Paphlagonian and Matieni contingents in Xerxes' invasion army.
per-artochmes: A Persian general commanding the Armenian and Phrygian contingents in Xerxes' invasion army, married to a daughter of Darius.
per-megasidrus: Father of Dotus, a Persian commander under Xerxes.
per-cherasmis: Father of Artayctes, who governed Sestus and commanded the Macrones and Mossynoeci in Xerxes' invasion army.
per-bassaces: Commander of the Asian Thracians (formerly called Strymonians) in Xerxes' invasion force, son of Artabanus.
per-harmamithres: A Persian cavalry captain, son of Datis, who served in Xerxes' invasion force of Greece.
per-ariazus: Father of Gergis, a Persian general in Xerxes' invasion force.
per-hystanes: Father of Badres, the commander of the Milyae and other peoples in Xerxes' army.
per-siromitres: A Persian, father of Masistius, who commanded the Alarodians and Saspires in Xerxes' invasion army.
per-tithaeus: One of the two cavalry captains in Xerxes' Persian army, son of Datis, who marched with the invasion force toward Greece.
per-cilix: Ancestor of the Cilicians, son of the Phoenician Agenor, from whom the Cilicians took their name.
per-calchas: A Greek soothsayer who, according to Herodotus, led Trojan refugees to Pamphylia after the fall of Troy.
per-tetramnestus: A Sidonian commander, son of Anysus, serving in Xerxes' naval forces during the invasion of Greece.
per-pharnuces: A Persian cavalry captain, son of Datis, who lost his command after being thrown from his horse at Sardis and becoming ill.
per-matten: Phoenician commander from Tyre serving in Xerxes' fleet during the invasion of Greece.
per-anysus: A man of Sidon whose son Tetramnestus served as a notable commander in Xerxes' fleet.
per-agbalus: A Phoenician, father of Merbalus who was an admiral from Aradus in Xerxes' fleet.
per-oromedon: Father of Syennesis, the Cilician commander in Xerxes' fleet.
per-merbalus: An Aradusian commander serving in Xerxes' fleet during the invasion of Greece.
per-cyberniscus: A Lycian, son of Sicas, among the notable commanders of Xerxes' fleet at the invasion of Greece.
per-sicas: Father of Cyberniscus, a Lycian commander in Xerxes' fleet.
per-timonax: A Cypriot naval commander, son of Timagoras, serving in Xerxes' fleet during the invasion of Greece.
per-timagoras: Father of Timonax, a Cypriot commander in Xerxes' fleet.
per-orgeus: Antipatrus son of Orgeus, a prominent Thasian whose father served as a notable citizen of Thasos.
per-megadostes: Father of Mascames, who was appointed governor of Doriscus by Xerxes.
per-antipatrus: A Thasian notable chosen to provide hospitality and provisions for Xerxes' army, who reported expenditures of four hundred silver talents for the entertainment.
per-aphytis: A town on the Pallene peninsula (formerly called Phlegra) that contributed ships and men to Xerxes' invading fleet.
per-megacreon: A citizen of Abdera who made a witty remark about the burden of provisioning Xerxes' army during its march through Thrace.
per-hysseldomus: Son of Hysseldomus, a Carian notable serving in Xerxes' fleet during the invasion of Greece.
per-nicolaus: Father of Bulis, a Spartan of noble birth whose son volunteered to atone for Sparta's killing of Persian heralds by traveling to Media for execution.
per-talthybiadae: Descendants of Talthybius (Agamemnon's herald), a family at Sparta granted the hereditary privilege of conducting all Spartan embassies.
per-aleues: A Thessalian dynastic family whose sons were the first Greeks to submit to Xerxes, whom Xerxes mistakenly believed represented their entire nation.
per-nicolas: Son of Bulis, Spartan ambassador to Asia with Aneristus, betrayed and seized by Thracian king Sitalces and put to death by the Athenians.
per-timon: A notable Delphian who advised the Athenian messengers at Delphi to approach the oracle a second time with suppliant boughs, resulting in the famous oracle concerning the wooden wall and Salamis.
per-aristonice: The Pythia (priestess) at Delphi who delivered an oracle to the Athenians during the Persian Wars, warning them to flee the city as it would be destroyed by fire and war.
per-nymphodorus: A Thracian of Abdera who, with King Sitalces, betrayed Lacedaemonian ambassadors to the Athenians during the Peloponnesian War.
per-tereus: A Thracian king, father of Sitalces, who betrayed Lacedaemonian ambassadors to the Athenians.
per-androbulus: Father of Timon, a Delphian notable; mentioned only in relation to his son's role in advising the Athenians to seek a second oracle at Delphi.
per-trito: The Trito-born is Athena, goddess of Athens, invoked in the Delphic oracle's prophecy of wooden walls as salvation for Athens against the Persian invasion.
per-dinomenes: Father of Gelon, ruler of Syracuse whose power was said to surpass any in Greece, mentioned when the Greeks seek aid from his son against Xerxes' invasion.
per-antiphemus: A colonist from Rhodes who, along with the Lindians, founded the city of Gela in Sicily.
per-pantares: Father of Cleandrus, tyrant of Gela.
per-pataecus: Father of Aenesidemus, a man of Gela whose son served in Hippocrates' guard.
per-euclides: Son of Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, whom Gelon deposed and replaced in power.
per-menestheus: Menestheus, legendary Athenian commander at Troy whom Homer praised as the finest marshal of armies, invoked by the Athenian envoy in 480 BC to justify Athens' claim to naval command against Gelon of Syracuse.
per-hiero: Brother of Gelon, left in charge of Gela while Gelon ruled Syracuse.
per-annon: King of Carthage and father of Amilcas, who led a massive North African and Mediterranean force against Sicily at the time of the Persian Wars.
per-choerus: Father of Micythus, who served as regent of Rhegium under Anaxilaus.
per-crinippus: Father of Terillus, the tyrant of Himera who was expelled by Theron of Acragas.
per-daedalus: A legendary craftsman of Crete whom King Minos pursued to Sicily, where Minos died in the attempt to capture him.
per-euaenetus: Spartan general chosen from the Polemarchs (not of royal house) who commanded the Greek land forces sent to defend the pass of Tempe against Xerxes' invasion.
per-carenus: Father of Euaenetus, a Lacedaemonian general at the pass of Tempe during Xerxes' invasion.
per-cydippe: Daughter of Terillus, tyrant of Himera, and wife of Anaxilaus of Rhegium, whose marriage led Anaxilaus to enlist Carthaginian aid for his father-in-law against Theron of Acragas.
per-polemarchs: Spartan military officers from whom a general (Euaenetus) was selected to command Greek forces at Tempe against the Persian invasion.
per-cephisus: Daughter of the river god Cephisus, associated with a precinct at Thyia near Delphi where the Greeks later erected an altar to the winds.
per-prexinus: Captain of the ship from Troezen whose vessel was captured by the Persian fleet during the naval campaign, after which the Persians executed one of his crew members as a sacrificial offering.
per-pammon: A man of Scyros who revealed to the Persian fleet the location of the reef in the strait during Xerxes' invasion of Greece.
per-cretines: Father of Ameinocles of Magnesia, whose son later profited from Persian shipwrecks at Sepia.
per-ameinocles: A man of Magnesia whose land bordered Sepia, he enriched himself by collecting Persian treasures and precious vessels washed ashore after the shipwreck of Xerxes' fleet.
per-asonides: Captain of an Aeginetan trireme during the naval battle at Salamis, commanding the ship on which the heroic Pytheas served.
per-thamasius: Father of Sandoces, viceroy of Cyme in Aeolia.
per-phormus: An Athenian captain whose trireme ran aground at the mouth of the Peneus while fleeing the Persians during Xerxes' invasion, allowing his crew to escape inland to Athens.
per-penthylus: A Paphian captain, son of Demonous, who lost eleven of his twelve ships in a storm off the Sepiad headland and was captured by the Greeks en route to Artemisium.
per-peleus: A legendary Greek hero who abducted the sea-nymph Thetis from the headland of Sepia in Thessaly, according to local Ionian tradition cited by Herodotus.
per-ino: A figure in Greek mythology, wife of Athamas, who plotted the death of Phrixus and became the subject of a cautionary tale related to Xerxes at Alus in Achaea.
per-amphictyon: A legendary or divine figure honoring whom the Amphictyonic League (a religious association of Greek states) held meetings at their sanctuary near Thermopylae in Locris.
per-laphystian-zeus: An Achean deity honored with human sacrifice of Phrixus' descendants at Alus, whose sanctuary Xerxes reverently avoided during his invasion of Greece.
per-eurycratides: A legendary ancestor of Leonidas in the Spartan royal line, appearing in the genealogy traced back through Heracles.
per-zeus-laphystius: A deity worshipped by the Achaeans at Alus, associated with a cult practice requiring descendants of Phrixus to undergo ritual sacrifice, which Xerxes chose to honor by avoiding the sacred precinct.
per-eurycrates: An ancestor of Leonidas in the Spartan royal line, several generations before the Persian Wars.
per-alcamenes: An ancestor of Leonidas in the Spartan royal line, many generations removed.
per-anaxandrus: An ancestor of Leonidas, king of Sparta, appearing in the genealogy tracing Leonidas' descent from Heracles.
per-teleclus: An ancestor of Leonidas, king of Sparta, in the genealogy tracing back through Spartan royal lineage to Heracles.
per-amphictyonid-demeter: A goddess, mother of Persephone, venerated at Anthele near Thermopylae where the Amphictyonic League held meetings and maintained a sanctuary.
per-archelaus: An ancestor of Leonidas in the Spartan royal line, several generations before Leonidas' time.
per-echestratus: An ancestor of Leonidas in the Spartan royal line, son of Agis.
per-leobotes: An ancestor of Leonidas in the Spartan royal line, several generations before the Persian Wars.
per-eurydemus: Father of Epialtes the Malian who betrayed the path over the mountain at Thermopylae.
per-doryssus: An ancestor of Leonidas in the Spartan royal line, grandfather of Leobotes.
per-demophilus: Thespian general commanding those who remained to die with Leonidas at Thermopylae.
per-heracleid: A Spartan royal clan to which Leonidas, commander of the Greek forces at Thermopylae, belonged.
per-phanagoras: Father of Onetes, a Carystian whom Herodotus rejects as the guide of the Persians around Mount Oeta during the invasion of Greece.
per-phratagune: Daughter of Artanes and mother of Abrocomes and Hyperanthes, two sons of Darius who fell at Thermopylae.
per-hyperanthes: A Persian, son of Darius and Phratagune, killed at Thermopylae during the battle against the Spartans.
per-abrocomes: Son of Darius and Phratagune, killed fighting at Thermopylae alongside his brother Hyperanthes.
per-diadromes: Father of Demophilus, the Thespian general who stayed to die with Leonidas at Thermopylae.
per-maron: Lacedaemonian brother of Alpheus, son of Orsiphantus, noted for courage at Thermopylae.
per-alpheus: Lacedaemonian brother of Maron, son of Orsiphantus, noted for courage at Thermopylae.
per-orsiphantus: Father of the Lacedaemonian brothers Alpheus and Maron, who distinguished themselves at Thermopylae.
per-dithyrambus: A Thespian warrior who was most renowned for his courage among the Greeks at Thermopylae.
per-harmatides: A Thespian whose son Dithyrambus distinguished himself among the Greeks fighting at Thermopylae.
per-pantites: One of the 300 Spartans at Thermopylae who survived by being sent as a messenger to Thessaly, and subsequently hanged himself in dishonor upon his return to Sparta.
per-aristodemus-the-trembler: A Spartan hoplite who survived the Battle of Thermopylae while his comrades died, earning the epithet "the Trembler" for his disgrace upon returning home, but later redeemed himself through distinguished valor at the Battle of Plataea.
per-aeschraeus: Athenian, father of Lycomedes, the first Greek to capture an enemy ship at the battle of Artemisium.
per-antidorus: A Greek from Lemnos fighting on the Persian side who deserted to the Greeks at Artemisium and was rewarded with land in Salamis by the Athenians.
per-lycomedes: An Athenian, son of Aeschraeus, who was the first Greek to capture an enemy ship at the battle of Artemisium and received the prize for valor.
per-philaon: Brother of Gorgus king of Salamis, a man of note in the Persian fleet, captured by the Greeks at the naval engagement off Artemisium.
per-athenians-clinias: An Athenian of wealth and distinction who equipped a trireme and two hundred men entirely at his own expense during Xerxes' invasion, and was distinguished for his valor in the sea-fight.
per-polyas: A Greek scout from Anticyra stationed at Artemisium with a boat ready to report any naval reverse to the hoplites at Thermopylae.
per-alcibiades: Son of Alcibiades, an Athenian who equipped his own ship and crew of two hundred men for the Greek fleet at Salamis.
per-lysicles: Father of Abronichus, an Athenian who served as a messenger between the Greek forces at Thermopylae and Artemisium during the Persian Wars.
per-aceratus: A prophet at Delphi who witnessed sacred arms miraculously appearing before the shrine of Athena Pronaea during the Persian advance.
per-herakles: A legendary hero who, together with the Malians, drove the Dryopians out of the region that became Doris.
per-phayllus: A Crotonian athlete, three-time victor at the Pythian games, who commanded his city's single ship in the Greek fleet against Xerxes' invasion.
per-democritus: A Naxian of repute who, as captain of a trireme, persuaded his fellow citizens to join the Greeks at Salamis against Persian orders.
per-calliades: Archon of Athens during the Persian invasion when Xerxes' army reached Attica and captured the city.
per-areopagus: A hill opposite the Athenian acropolis where Persian forces took position during the siege of Athens in 480 BC.
per-aglaurus: A daughter of Cecrops, an Athenian heroine whose sacred precinct on the acropolis was near a steep cliff where Persian forces climbed during the assault on Athens in 480 BC.
per-telamon: Son of Aeacus; invoked as a protective ally by the Greek fleet at Salamis before the battle against Xerxes' Persian forces.
per-earthborn: Erechtheus, a deity worshipped at Athens as an autochthonous king and culture-hero, represented in the Acropolis shrine alongside symbols of Poseidon and Athena's contest for Attica.
per-pisistratids: Athenian tyrants whose descendants resisted Persian siege on the Acropolis during Xerxes' invasion, initially proposing surrender terms that the defenders rejected.
per-sosimenes: Father of Panaetius, a Tenian naval captain who deserted to the Greeks during the Persian Wars.
per-panaetius: Captain of a Tenian trireme who deserted to the Greeks at Salamis and reported the Persian fleet's movements.
per-eumenes: An Athenian from Anagyrus distinguished for courage in the naval battle at Salamis against Xerxes' fleet.
per-aminias: An Athenian from Pallene who pursued the ship of Artemisia, the Persian queen, during the naval battle in the Histories' account of the Persian Wars.
per-hippocratides: An ancestor of the Spartan king Leutychides, appearing in his genealogy tracing back to Heracles.
per-lysistratus: An Athenian soothsayer whose oracle about wrecks washing ashore at Colias was fulfilled after Salamis, though its meaning was obscure to the Greeks until the event occurred.
per-eunomus: An early king of Sparta, ancestor of Leutychides in the Eurypontid line.
per-timodemus: An Athenian from Aphidnae who envied Themistocles and taunted him upon his return from Sparta, only to be silenced by Themistocles' sharp retort.
per-theopompus: An early Spartan king in the ancestral lineage of Leutychides, traced back through generations to Heracles' son Hyllus.
per-athena-sciras: A sanctuary on the island of Salamis where, according to Athenian accounts, a mysterious boat appeared during the naval battle to turn back the fleeing Corinthian ships.
per-polydectes: An ancient Spartan king in the lineage of Leutychides, tracing descent through multiple generations to Heracles' son Hyllus.
per-nicandrus: An ancestor of Leutychides II in the Spartan royal genealogy, several generations before the Persian Wars.
per-euryphon: Ancestor of the Spartan king Leutychides, placed in the genealogy between Prytanis and Procles.
per-prytanis: An ancestor in the legendary Spartan royal genealogy, appearing in the lineage of Leutychides son of Menares.
per-basileides: Father of Herodotus of Chios, an Ionian conspirator against the tyrant Strattis who fled to Sparta and then Aegina to urge the Greeks to aid Ionia.
per-silenus: A satyr or divine being captured in the garden of Midas in Macedonia, according to Macedonian tradition.
per-ptoan-apollo: A god worshipped at a sanctuary near Acraephia in Boeotia, whose oracle delivered a prophecy in Carian when visited by Mys of Europus during the Persian Wars.
per-phrynon: Father of Attaginus, a Theban who hosted Mardonius and Persian nobles at a banquet before Plataea.
